events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9��Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ��———————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description: The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.title: Exhibit | De y para el pueblo / By and for the People: Revolutionary Mexican Prints
events.description: The exhibit features highlights from The Bancroft Library's extensive collection of prints. The show examines how a Mexico City-based artists collective, the Taller de Gráfica Popular (Workshop for Popular Graphic Art), built an artistic legacy, tracing its roots from José Guadalupe Posada's portrayals of everyday Mexican life, to its enduring influence on artists on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border today.

events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibit | Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Bernice Layne Brown Gallery (inside Doe Library)
events.description: In August 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with youth and elders from the nation's Indigenous communities. That expedition, Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here (https://www.ourlifeishere.org), was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. An exhibition in Doe Library's Bernice Layne Brown Gallery gathers reproductions of works made during and after the voyage together with rare books, maps, and photographs drawn from UC Berkeley's own libraries—The Bancroft Library, the Earth Sciences & Map Library, the Environmental Design Library, Morrison Library, and the Main (Gardner) Stacks. Six cases move from the conditions that shaped the voyage, through the journey itself, to the living Marshallese knowledge and youth-led activism that carry it forward. Interpretive text is punctuated by QR codes linking to films, poems, and the organizations at the center of the project. This presentation is part of a series of exhibitions, installations, courses, and public programs across UC Berkeley during the 2026–27 academic year (https://cici.berkeley.edu/komij-mour-ijin-our-life-here-uc-berkeley), guided by the Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative. The exhibition was co-curated by independent curators Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll, in partnership with UC Berkeley librarians Becky Miller and Susan Powell. The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell.

events.title: Photography Installation: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands
events.description: At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. An artist and curator-led tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox will take place on September 23 at 4 PM. —Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books. Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. —Presented by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative in partnership with the Rausser College of Natural Resources.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation. —Image Credit: "The concrete bunker destroyed by the 15-megaton Bravo explosion"2023. events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. events.title: BTLJ-BCLT Fall Race & Law Symposium – "Being Human in the Age of AI"
events.description: Join us for Being Human in the Age of AI, a symposium exploring how artificial intelligence is reshaping the law's most basic assumptions about the human person — from the privacy of the mind to the boundaries of legal responsibility. Across four panels, we trace an arc from the innermost self outward: how neurotechnology and algorithmic design test the limits of cognitive liberty; how deepfakes and biometric systems unsettle the law of identity; how automated decision-making challenges due process and the right to be heard; and how courts and legislatures are struggling to define what AI fundamentally is. Attendees will hear from leading scholars, technologists, and practitioners grappling with these questions in real time, as courts issue rulings, states pass conflicting statutes, and AI companies themselves debate the moral status of the systems they build.

events.title: Book Launch: "Russia's New Imperialism"
events.description: Russia's devastating invasion of Ukraine in 2022 is a manifestation of a wider phenomenon: Russia's new, post-Soviet imperialism. This book provides a theoretically informed, critical account of Russian imperialism that is attentive to the interplay between economy and ideology, coercion and hegemony, structure and agency. While economic developments go a long way toward explaining the reemergence of Russia's imperialist impulses in the twenty-first century, a purely economic logic cannot account for the dramatic shift in Russian imperialism beginning with the annexation of Crimea and the instigation of a separatist insurgency in the Donbas. Nor can objective geopolitical developments, such as US and NATO military deployments, provide an adequate explanation for this shift. Instead, this book shows how the Kremlin's reaction to the Maidan revolution was rooted in the ideological consolidation of the previous years: the emergence of a total ideology that designates the West as Russia's eternal enemy and Ukraine as the West's geopolitical pawn. Ilya Budraitskis and Ilya Matveev examine Russian foreign policy and the Kremlin's project to remake the Russian people to better serve its imperialist agenda.

events.title: Florentin Guth: How many effective parameters do deep networks learn from data?
events.description: A central puzzle in deep learning is that neural networks can generalize despite having many billions of parameters. This suggests that through implicit regularization, deep networks may only learn a smaller number of effective parameters from data. We propose to estimate it from the dimensionality (rank) of the learned weight matrices. I will show that the empirical behavior of this quantity is consistent with what we expect from an effective parameter count, both qualitatively and quantitatively. In particular, it satisfies surprisingly simple scaling laws when the number of training steps, neurons, and data samples are increased, which provide a direct window into generalization and memorization. In fact, its behavior is very similar to a central and well-understood quantity in the simpler setting of ridge regression, known as the degrees of freedom (also called learnability). These tantalizing parallels suggest a potential path towards a theory of deep learning. Friday, October 16, 2026Time: 11:00 AMLocation: Warren Hall 205AZoom: Join Zoom Meeting (https://berkeley.zoom.us/j/91260194773)Speaker:Florentin Guth (https://florentinguth.github.io/)Affiliations:Flatiron Institute (https://www.simonsfoundation.org/flatiron/center-for-computational-neuroscience/), MIT (https://www.csail.mit.edu/)

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Dr. Wenbing Yang, Lam Research | Plasma Atomic Layer Etch
events.description: Abstract: As transistor technology scales toward the angstrom node, an increasing number of semiconductor fabrication processes require atomic-scale control. The era of atomic-scale engineering presents unprecedented challenges and opportunities for advancing semiconductor fabrication technology. Through self-limiting surface reactions, atomic layer etching (ALE) provides precision control to address these demands. ALE has been proven to enable many etch steps in new device architectures and integration schemes that were previously infeasible. This talk will provide an introduction for plasma enhanced atomic layer etch, focus on the fundamentals and development of ALE using silicon case study. Additional examples will illustrate ALE for a range of materials and applications, demonstrate its potential to support advanced semiconductor devices and manufacturing strategy. Bio: Dr. Wenbing Yang is a Technical Director in the Pathfinding Group in the Office of the CTO at Lam Research. At Lam Research, he led the development of plasma-enhanced atomic layer etching (ALE), brining it from lab to fab on the Kiyo® conductor etch platform for volume manufacturing. As transistor technology advances into the Å node, his work focuses on critical applications that require atomic scale process control. As an atom engineer, he holds over 50 patents in the field of atomic scale engineering, process development, and technology integration. Wenbing has a B.S. from USTC, and a Ph.D. from UCLA.

events.title: Gerardo Aldana | Sak Tahn Waax, Astronomy, and Psychedelics in the History of Mayan Oracular Science
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.location: Latinx Research Center, 2547 Channing Way, Berkeley
events.description: Event Description Science is often thought of as a European development. The Mayan civilization had thousands of years of astronomical and scientific developments marginalized by colonial expansion in the early modern period. Well before the Spanish invasion, Mayan and Mesoamerican cultures were developing sophisticated scientific, medical, calendrical and mathematical frameworks that have yet to be integrated into the discussion of what constitutes advanced scientific thinking. Through the history of Mayan astronomy, we can capture dimensions of these non-European scientific developments, native to the Americas, that deserve to be revitalized and historically understood in their own cultural context.Part of the CLACS Historically Situating Mayan Scientific Knowledge event series, supported by CLACS. Co-sponsored by the Center for Science, Technology, Medicine, and Society; the Latinx Research Center; Chicanx Latinx Studies; the Department of Anthropology, the Department of History; and the Department of Astronomy. Speaker Gerardo Aldana is a Professor of Chicana and Chicano Studies at UC Santa Barbara and a historian of science specializing in Maya astronomy, hieroglyphic history, and Indigenous intellectual traditions. Trained in both mechanical engineering and the history of science, Aldana earned his Ph.D. from Harvard University and brings interdisciplinary approaches from history, archaeology, astronomy, and science studies to the study of Mesoamerica and Maya astronomy. His 2022 book, Calculating Brilliance: An Intellectual History of Mayan Astronomy at Chich'en Itza, reframes Maya astronomy as a sophisticated Indigenous intellectual tradition by reanalyzing one of the few surviving Maya texts, the Dresden Codex, which articulates robust astronomical and mathematical knowledge.

events.title: Matthew Parker (Informal BBS Seminar): Adaptive evolution of Orc1's disordered region rewires chromatin recognition and origin specification in metazoans
events.description: Sites of DNA replication initiation are specified by binding of the origin recognition complex (ORC, composed of Orc1–6) to particular chromosomal loci, but how metazoan ORC selects these sites remains poorly understood. I will discuss our work defining the mechanisms by which ORC engages chromatin in human cells and Drosophila, focusing on an Orc1 intrinsically disordered region (IDR) that mediates genomic site selection. Extending these studies across metazoans, we find that an Orc1 IDR is universally retained but has evolved under positive selection, producing distinct sequence architectures with functional consequences for DNA-binding specificity and sites of replication initiation.This seminar is partially sponsored by NIHDivision(s): Division of Biochemistry, Biophysics and Structural Biology

A presidential election will follow by the end of December, after President Vuči�� resigned in September to run for prime minister. A list emerging from the student movement leads in independent polling, and most opposition parties have stepped back to support it. It will contest seats against a party that has, over the past decade, consolidated control over broadcast media, the security apparatus, electoral administration, the public sector and the regulatory bodies. The conditions are heavily uneven. National broadcasters and the tabloid press are aligned with the ruling party, while the regulatory bodies that might act as a corrective to this have repeatedly declined to act. Public funds, public employment and public contracts are used as leverage on voters. Questions about the accuracy of the voter register remain unresolved from previous cycles. International observers have issued the same recommendations election after election, and they have gone largely unimplemented. Recent local elections were marked by intimidation, and in some places by open violence at polling stations. The last major group of media not aligned with the government has changed hands to investment vehicles that have bought critical outlets elsewhere, only to quietly end their criticism. Despite this, the outcome is not settled, and the election is worth watching closely. This panel brings together Serbian civil society organizations working on election observation and investigative journalism, along with a political sociologist who has written on Serbia's captured institutions, its elections, and social movements. Nine days before the parliamentary vote, it asks what conditions are like on the ground and what is at stake. This event is co-sponsored by the Democracy Action Lab at the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL) and the Center for Russian, East European and Eurasian Studies at Stanford. For more information and to register for the event, visit CDDRL at Stanford (https://cddrl.fsi.stanford.edu/events/captured-field-open-contest-serbias-upcoming-elections).

events.title: Glenn T. Seaborg Memorial Lectures in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Erwin Reisner, Professor of Energy and Sustainability, University of CambridgeSemi-artificial Photosynthesis using Formate Dehydrogenase Semi-artificial photosynthesis interfaces biological catalysts with synthetic light absorbers to overcome the inherent limitations of both artificial and natural photosynthesis. Furthermore, this emerging approach can also unlock novel reaction pathways and chemistries with significant technological potential and thus provides new opportunities that are currently not available in solar fuels or algae research. This presentation will summarise our progress in integrating the redox enzyme formate dehydrogenase into bespoke hierarchical 3D electrode scaffolds, photoelectrodes and semiconductor powders. Specifically, formate dehydrogenase immobilised on electrodes enables catalytic CO₂ reduction to formate with electrochemical reversibility and can thus operate at very low overpotential with high selectivity. The design principles for the integration of formate dehydrogenase in bespoke synthetic 3D electrode scaffolds and a detailed analysis of the biocatalyst-material interface will be presented. The understanding of the biotic-abiotic interface ultimately allows for the rational wiring of the biocatalyst into photoelectrochemical and photocatalytic systems for the solar synthesis of fuels and chemicals. Overall, the lecture aims to demonstrate that formate dehydrogenase should be considered as unique model electrocatalyst for CO₂-to-formate conversion in solar catalysis as it enables performance currently not achievable by synthetic catalysts. A recent review on this topic is available: Liu et al., Chem. Rev., 2026, 126, 8034–8088 (https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.6c00095).

events.title: Dissertation Talk: Generative Models for Human and Robot Action
events.description: Recent progress in machine learning, computer vision, and robot hardware has brought down fundamental barriers to building intelligent embodied agents. In this talk, I'll present my work on using diffusion and flow-based generative models to solve a complementary pair of such problems: first in an estimation setting, where we propose a system for scalably collecting human action data from egocentric devices, and second in a control setting, where we introduce an online reinforcement learning algorithm for training more expressive robot policies. I'll conclude with broader thoughts.

events.title: Student Probability/PDE Seminar: The KPZ Fixed Point and the Directed Landscape VI
events.description: Speaker: Fraydoun Rezakhanlou, UC BerkeleyThe KPZ equation was proposed in 1986 by Kardar, Parisi and Zhang as a model for stochastic growth interfaces. It is conjectured that many stochastic height functions will converge to KPZ fixed point under 1:2:3 scaling. Simultaneous construction of KPZ fixed points for different initial data yields the directed landscape. events.title: Toward Trustworthy (Automated Driving) Companies
events.description: Bryant Walker Smith, Associate Professor of Law and (by courtesy) Engineering at University of South Carolina, will present Toward Trustworthy (Automated Driving) Companies at the ITS Berkeley Transportation Seminar on Oct. 16, 2026 at 3 pm. Join us for cookie hour in the ITS Library at 2:30 p.m. Abstract: There are no "driverless" or "self-driving" vehicles. Rather, these vehicles are driven by the companies developing and deploying them. A handful of corporate drivers might one day replace hundreds of millions of human drivers. This centralization of power could have profound consequences for individuals, communities, governments, and companies–and particularly for the relationships among them. My talk uses this spectrum of control, from distributed to concentrated, to consider the responsibilities of both developers and regulators. Incidental tasks once performed by human drivers might be shifted to others, their costs externalized, or the associated responsibilities abdicated. Federal regulatory authority over the design of motor vehicles might extend to every operational decision. Close coordination between regulators and developers could threaten individual autonomy. I argue for treating safety–broadly understood–as an ongoing commitment rather than merely a one-time test; for assessing safety in part through the trustworthiness of those deploying automated vehicles and other AI systems; for empowering new forms of collectives; and, ultimately, for expecting more from all those with power. Bio: Bryant Walker Smith is an associate professor in the School of Law and (by courtesy) the College of Engineering and Computing at the University of South Carolina, as well as an affiliate scholar (https://cyberlaw.stanford.edu/bws) at the Center for Internet and Society at Stanford Law School. In 2025, he was a visiting professor (https://newlypossible.org/files/presentations/2025-06-28_FutureHumanitySpeech_BryantWalkerSmith.pdf) at Renmin University of China. Trained as a lawyer and an engineer, Smith advises cities, states, countries, and the United Nations on artificial intelligence, automated driving, and other emerging technologies. He has testified before the US Senate Commerce Committee (https://cyberlaw.stanford.edu/blog/2026/02/opening-statement-of-professor-bryant-walker-smith-for-the-u-s-senate-commerce-committees-hearing-on-automated-driving-february-4-2026-2/), vice-chaired the US Department of Transportation's Transforming Transportation Advisory Committee (https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/2025-01/TTAC%202024%20Report.pdf), served as an expert witness (https://www.plainsite.org/dockets/download.html?id=361671590&z=0992d8f5) for the State of California, coauthored the globally influential levels of driving automation (https://www.sae.org/standards/j3016_202104-taxonomy-definitions-terms-related-driving-automation-systems-road-motor-vehicles), drafted a ULC model law (https://www.uniformlaws.org/committees/community-home?CommunityKey=4e70cf8e-a3f4-4c55-9d27-fb3e2ab241d6) for automated driving, and (in 2012) taught the first legal course dedicated to automated driving. Smith's article on "The Trustworthy Company" is forthcoming in the Georgetown Law Journal, and his article on "Regulating Robotaxis" is forthcoming in the Southern California Law Review. His publications are available at newlypossible.org (http://newlypossible.org/). Before joining the University of South Carolina, Smith led the legal aspects of automated driving program at Stanford University, clerked for the Hon. Evan J. Wallach at the United States Court of International Trade, and worked as a fellow at the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. He holds both an LL.M. in International Legal Studies and a J.D. (cum laude) from New York University School of Law and a B.S. in Civil Engineering from the University of Wisconsin. Prior to his legal career, Smith worked as a transportation engineer.

events.description: The UC Berkeley Department of German and BAMPFA are pleased to host Stefanie Schulte Strathaus's Mosse Lecture. She will speak about the international collaborations she is involved with through her position as Artistic Director of the Arsenal Filminstitut in Berlin and across a career that has been devoted to film curation, restoration projects, and developing partnerships with film communities in Egypt and Nigeria. Schulte Strathaus served on the selection committee of the Berlinale Forum and was the Founding Director of the Berlinale section Forum Expanded. Two of her signature accomplishments are the development of the Living Archive project at Arsenal Filminstitut and launching the biennial festival Archival Assembly. This annual lecture is generously supported by the Mosse Foundation and reflects the foundation's mission to promote cultural exchange and political engagement. The Mosse Lectures were originally founded in 1997 at Humboldt University in Berlin to commemorate the history of the Mosse family, their patronage of the arts, and their contributions to intellectual life through the German-Jewish publishing house run by Rudolf Mosse and the newspaper Berliner Tageblatt.

events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Castrato Phantoms Book Chat w/ Martha Feldman (University of Chicago)
events.description: Castrato PhantomsBook ChatMartha Feldman (University of Chicago) Held in the Townsend Center's Geballe RoomMartha Feldman (Ferdinand Schevill Distinguished Service Professor, Music & Theater and Performance Studies, University of Chicago) discusses her sweeping account of the castrato dilemma in its end stages as an index of modern consciousness. How can we write the histories of a complex multigenerational past when it is mired in obfuscations that stretch from the most intimate of family events to the doings of the Roman church to the machinery of the Italian state? This was the challenge Feldman faced when she crossed paths with descendants of the last castrato to star in Roman chapels, whose uncle turned out to be the iconic film director Federico Fellini. Some years after their first encounter, she offers a book that unravels the entanglements of family traumas with the secret suppressions of the Vatican and fascist state. Her Castrato Phantoms: Moreschi, Fellini, and the Sacred Vernacular in Rome (Zone Books, 2026) provides compelling answers that follow up on her Berkeley Bloch Lectures (published as The Castrato: Reflections on Natures and Kinds, University of California Press, 2015). Her novel concept of the sacred vernacular makes sense of the profanations of everyday sacred rituals and objects, traced here through sound recordings, literary texts, photographs, films, and letters. Drawing on Roman archives, a previously unknown family archive, and a wealth of Roman historical documentation, she deploys the sacred vernacular to rewrite the history of old-world hauntings in a modern key. Feldman will deliver a half-hour lecture before conversing with Prof. James Q. Davies. A Q & A with the audience will follow. Prof. Ramona Naddaff will moderate.

events.title: Film Screening: Raging Bull
events.description: Martin Scorsese and Robert De Niro make the biography of boxer Jake LaMotta into a visceral meditation on existential suffering. Eschewing the romance associated with the sport, Raging Bull shows the struggle of an athlete whose willful determination to succeed on his own terms takes its toll on all those around him—friends and adversaries in equal measure—before he is undermined by self-loathing. Every punch is framed, lit, and cut for maximum impact, with black-and-white cinematography inspired by James Wong Howe. "A fusion of Hollywood genre with personal vision . . . closer to poetry than pulp. Its sculptural weight can only be appreciated on the big screen" (Amy Taubin, Village Voice).

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

events.title: Language & Literacy across the Disciplines
events.description: Language and literacy are embedded in every subject students encounter. This Saturday Seminar is an opportunity for TK-12 educators from across the Bay Area to strengthen language and literacy practices in their classrooms. Saturday Seminars are led by UC Berkeley's content area experts, who represent California Subject Matter Project sites and partner organizations in the field of education. Workshops are teacher-centered professional learning spaces that emphasize practical tools, approaches, and strategies to bring to classrooms on Monday! Session 1 Workshops 9:15 - 10:45 AMScience and Literacy: Speaking, Writing & Reading to Learn Science (k-5) We often think of literacy and science as academic opposites. But we can't do science without reading, writing, listening, and communicating. This workshop will focus participants on two questions: In what ways can learning science develop students' language skills? and, How do language skills support sense-making in science? Teachers will engage in a shared learning experience using a classroom science activity, and engage in a debrief discussion, examining interconnections of science and literacy. This workshop is most applicable for elementary school teachers, but all are welcome! Sarah Pedemonte currently serves as Director of the Bay Area Science Project. She has worked at the Lawrence Hall of Science for over 20 years, designing curriculum and facilitating professional learning for K-12 teachers in science.Place-Based Literacy: Exploring Local Infrastructures to Understand Global Topics (6-12) Our infrastructures reveal our connections to the broader world, our local social relations and political structures, our histories, our values, and more. This workshop introduces the concept of infrastructures and models lessons through which students can actively engage with the infrastructures that affect their own lives. Participants will also be introduced to a set of teacher-produced lessons for middle and high school students. Materials are drawn from a year-long program supported by California Global Education Project and ORIAS. Shane Carter is the Program Coordinator for ORIAS (the Office of Resources for International and Area Studies) at the University of California, Berkeley and a host-site director for California Global Education Project. In both roles Shane introduces educators to a range of international topics and provides them with tools to help students develop global competence. Shane is a former high school history-social studies teacher and the creator of two podcasts: Points In Between and Future Imperfect.Elizabeth Aracic has taught English and Social Studies for over 23 years at Miramonte High School in Orinda. She has taught 14 courses and was also librarian, and is always open to sharing curriculum (and never minds if you adapt it and make it your own). Suzy Anderson has taught seventh grade World History and English for 25 years at Mill Valley Middle School, and for the last few years has taught the Global Studies elective, focusing on sustainable development. Engaging Language Learners from the Start: Comprehensible Input and Guided Practice (TK-12) In this workshop, teachers will experience a short, comprehensible input story about choosing the ingredients for a salad. They will participate in guided practice activities to process the new material, practicing communicative language and literacy strategies to engage students. Nancy Salsig is Co-Director of the Berkeley World Language Project at UC Berkeley. She taught high school French and Spanish for 36 years. Currently she supervises student teachers at CSU East Bay and St. Mary's College.Who's in the Lead? Building Student Criticality about AI with the 4D Framework (6-12) AI literacy requires more than knowing how to use a tool. It requires students to question when AI should be used, how it works, whose experiences shape it, and how its decisions affect people. In this interactive workshop, participants will apply the 4D Framework, Determination, Data, Design, and Deployment, to realistic classroom scenarios across the grade spans. Participants will collaborate to identify bias, examine tradeoffs, and consider where human judgment must remain in the lead. Participants will leave with a practical questioning routine and adaptable prompts that help students evaluate AI critically, ethically, and equitably while preserving productive struggle and learner agency. This workshop is designed for 5th to 12th grade teachers, instructional coaches, and teacher leaders across content areas. All are welcome. Vanessa Lujan, Ph.D. is Director of K-12 STEM Education at the Lawrence Hall of Science. Vanessa brings deep expertise in K-12 STEM systems change, equity-centered leadership, and professional learning that helps districts bridge from vision to classroom practice. Her work focuses on building district capacity for STEM education while advancing learning environments where all students can see themselves as capable STEM thinkers and problem solvers.Eric Greenwald, Ph.D., Learning Sciences Researcher at the Lawrence Hall of Science, leads projects that advance research, learning design, and systems change at the intersection of science, math, computational thinking, and AI. In particular, he studies how learning can be designed toward a more robust and equitable socio-technical understanding of AI systems that better positions learners for criticality and agency in a world we are increasingly living together with AI.Crystal Menzies, Ph.D., Equity Research & Learning Systems Lead at the Lawrence Hall of Science, brings a scholar-practitioner perspective rooted in asset-based research, curriculum design, and professional learning to the AI K-12 Network team Session 2 Workshops 11:00 AM - 12:30 PMUsing Visual Historical Evidence to Support Analytical Thinking (6-12) This workshop focuses on using visual sources to analyze historical narratives with middle and high school History-Social Science students. Teachers will discuss a theoretical framework used for analyzing evidence, and the classroom inquiries this framework can inspire. Teachers will leave with at least 2 concrete strategies for analyzing images and realia that connect to structured academic conversation as well as focused content readings. Jason Muñiz is Director of the UC Berkeley History-Social Science Project. During his time with the project he has led the development of UCBHSSP's programmatic support for implementing Ethnic Studies by leading professional development for administrators and educators, developing interdisciplinary History-Social Science curriculum, and spearheading an initiative to bring UC Berkeley's Ethnic Studies and History institutional resources to High School teachers.Building Language, Ideas, and Sense of Self through Writing (6-12) Writing is a powerful medium for exploring ideas in all disciplines, making connections, and building language. In this workshop, participants will write for themselves, explore ways to embed writing across disciplines, and analyze multilingual students' writing for what it reveals about language practice. This workshop is best suited for secondary teachers, but all are welcome! Hillary Walker is Director of the Bay Area Writing Project (BAWP), which focuses on strengthening writing instruction in classrooms by sharing the expertise of writing teachers. She is a veteran secondary writing teacher, and also teaches community college courses in African American Studies, Ethnic Studies, and History.Metacognition: Making Meaning of Language by Making Thinking Visible (TK-12) So much of literacy is about making our thinking visible, identifying what our brains are doing as we encounter language, text, media, and the world around us. Metacognition is a deeply transferable skill that invites all learners to pause, to uncover what is normally invisible (even to ourselves), and thus to understand when/how we are accessing information and making meaning, and when/how we are getting stuck. Participants will connect with their personal metacognitive/reflective practices, explore and experience several research-based metacognitive strategies, and complete a mini-design sprint to incorporate a strategy into an upcoming lesson/unit/project. This session is applicable to TK-12 teachers and leaders, all are welcome! Abby Benedetto, College & Career Alliance Support Network (CCASN), has taken on designing and changing systems for the last two decades from a wide variety of roles and perspectives. Abby is able to draw upon her lived experience of the decade she spent as a classroom teacher and leader, a decade of working shoulder to shoulder with educators in this country and abroad, as well as a unique ability to help educators make connections between what they know and their aspirational vision for where they want to go. Abby is proud to serve as one of CCASN's lead collaborative partners.Dr. Tameka L. McGlawn, Executive Director and Principal Investigator, College & Career Alliance Support Network (CCASN), is a fourth-generation educator, scholar, counselor, and servant leader with more than 30 years of experience advancing educational equity through research, practice, policy, and systems leadership. She partners with district systems, networks, institutions, and organizations to strengthen leadership capacity and support sustainable and measurable transformation. She helps education leaders translate research into practical strategies that strengthen equity, coherence, and continuous improvement.Scaffolding Authentic Resources for All Learners (TK-12) Explore strategies to scaffold authentic resources to engage students. Learn how to make real-world texts accessible and meaningful to learners at all levels. The workshop centers on culturally responsive strategies across cultures. Nancy Salsig is Co-Director of the Berkeley World Language Project at UC Berkeley. She taught high school French and Spanish for 36 years. events.title: Pablo Leon | Silenced Voices: Reclaiming Memories from the Guatemalan Genocide
events.organizer: Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies
events.description: Event Description Join us online for the presentation of the Américas Award to author Pablo Leon for his young adult book Silenced Voices: Reclaiming Memories from the Guatemalan Genocide. Leon will read an excerpt from Silenced Voices and share insights about his writing process and bringing Central American stories into the classroom. The 45-minute ceremony will be held on Zoom on Saturday, October 17 at 9:30 am PT / 11:30 am CT / 12:30 pm ET. It is free and open to the public. The event is hosted by the Américas Award in collaboration with Teaching for Change's Teaching Central America program. The Américas Award for Children's and Young Adult Literature was founded in 1993 by the Consortium of Latin American Studies Programs (CLASP), of which Berkeley CLACS is a member. The Award commends authors, illustrators, and publishers who produce quality children's and young adult books that portray Latin America, the Caribbean, or Latinos in the United States, and to provide teachers with recommendations for classroom use. CLASP offers up to two annual book awards, together with a commended list of titles. By linking the Americas, the intent is to reach beyond geographic borders, focusing instead upon cultural heritages within the hemisphere.Presented by the Consortium of Latin American Studies Programs, coordinated by Tulane University's Stone Center for Latin American Studies and Vanderbilt University's Center for Latin American, Caribbean, and Latinx Studies, and supported by Berkeley CLACS.Speaker Pablo Leon is an author and artist from Guatemala, currently living in Los Angeles and jumping between TV animation and comics. He's an Eisner Award Nominee for his original comic "The Journey," an account of an unaccompanied child coming from Central America to the United States, and he was the illustrator for the exciting middle grade graphic novel series Miles Morales at Scholastic. His passion for capturing historical memory in his art and stories has led him to his writer/artist debut Silenced Voices: Reclaiming Memories from the Guatemalan Genocide: A Graphic Novel at HarperAlley Books, and his first animated short film Remember Us, which qualified for consideration for Best Animated Short Film for the Academy Awards.

events.title: La maison des bois: Episodes 1–3
events.description: Epic yet intimate, sweeping yet personal, La maison des bois stands as one of the greatest achievements in the history of television, as well as legendary director Maurice Pialat's magnum opus. Commissioned for Télévision Française in 1971, this seven-episode, nearly four-hundred-minute miniseries considers the impact of World War I on a simple French family living in the countryside. Applying a naturalistic focus to their subject, Pialat and screenwriter René Wheeler capture both the historical scope of the conflict and the subtle ways that a small town's quotidian routines and rituals—church, school, tavern—are indelibly touched by it.

events.title: Film Screening: White Nights
events.description: This adaptation of Fyodor Dostoyevsky's tale about displaced, disconnected people drifting along crossing, doubling paths was shot in moody black-and-white on a soundstage simulacrum of Livorno, Italy. With it Luchino Visconti veered away from verisimilitude and toward an emphatically subjective style—from neorealism to neoromanticism. As a quiet man who accidentally befriends a troubled, lonely young woman (Maria Schell) and finds himself playing understudy for the absent object of her affections (Jean Marais), Marcello Mastroianni mingles subtly passionate yearnings with a characteristic note of annoyance. His character is both distrustful of and seduced by the romantic dreams that preoccupy the woman he loves.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

events.title: BAMPFA Exhibition: Private Frontiers: Media Legacies of the Cold War
events.description: On display from Sep 9 - Dec 13, 2026 | 11 am - 7 p.m. Bookended by the end of World War II in 1945 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the Cold War was a transformative period in global history, marking both the end of the twentieth century and the waning of modernism. Though earlier historians defined the Cold War as the noncombative contest between the capitalist United States and the communist Soviet Union, recent interventions by scholars, artists, and writers have stressed that this period was also defined by the struggles for decolonization and national liberation movements across Asia and globally. Undeniable to the history of the Cold War is the crucial role that culture played in shaping perceptions of individuals, nations, and the global order, circulated through media such as international magazines, photographs, and television.Private Frontiers presents new and recent work in photography, video, and installation by contemporary artists who critically engage the Cold War as a prism for understanding today's media-saturated world. Through their methodologically-driven practices, artists Naeem Mohaiemen, Prajakta Potnis, TJ Shin, and Tiffany Sia draw on a range of references—including historical archives, news broadcasts, pop songs, and game theory—to critically examine media as a crucial arena in which politics was articulated and contested in the second half of the twentieth century. By looking carefully at how art and politics were entwined in the media of the past, these artists offer a way for us to carefully engage with the politics and art of our contemporary moment. Curated by Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator, and Atreyee Gupta (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/atreyee-gupta), Associate Professor, Department of History of Art, UC Berkeley, in conjunction with the undergraduate class HA37: Contemporary Art + Architecture from Asia, c. 1945–Present. (https://classes.berkeley.edu/content/2022-fall-histart-37-001-lec-001) Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATES: Sept 9–Dec 13, 2026 VENUE: BAMPFA HOURS: Wed-Sun, 11 AM–7 PM (Mon and Tues closed) TICKETS: Buy tickets HERE (https://bampfa.org/visit/hours) ——————���—- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952). events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. These exhibitions relied on its extensive, and ever-growing, holdings of art, books, manuscripts, and material culture, as well as different modalities in which these materials can be studied and displayed: from curatorial and scholarly forays into the collection to research projects created in collaboration with UC Berkeley Graduate and Undergraduate students, to real-life experiments with ideas borne out of courses and seminars. Each exhibition featured in Time Capsules is unique in exploring the cultures of the Jews in a global perspective, in bringing museum objects "back to life," and in offering ever-changing ways to understand the past in order to inform the future.Exhibition Team:Francesco Spagnolo and Shir Gal Kochavi, CuratorsZoe Foster, Undergraduate Curatorial ApprenticeJulie Franklin, RegistrarErnest Jolly, Head PreparatorCarole Jeung, Designer Located in downtown Berkeley, just steps from campus, the museum and research center is home to one of the world's preeminent collections of Jewish art and life. events.title: TEDxBerkeley 2026
events.location: Pauley Ballroom; 2495 Bancroft Way Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Every experiment begins with a question: What if? Experimentation launches us on a new journey into the unknown. Every trial, whether it leads to success, failure, or something in between, becomes a part of the discovery process. Xperiment is about leaning into uncertainty with intention; trying what hasn't been tried, breaking patterns, and embracing curiosity without the promise of a clear outcome. Just as a lab experiment requires curiosity, design and iteration, so do the choices we make in our lives, communities, and fields of work. Sometimes we follow a precise method; other times we stumble into accidental breakthroughs. At times our results can confirm our expectations, while at others they challenge us to rethink everything. But regardless of the result, each trial moves us closer to new ways of thinking or being. At TEDxBerkeley 2026: Xperiment, we invite you to challenge assumptions, explore unfamiliar ideas, and embrace the uncertainty that comes with trying something new. From bold discoveries to unexpected turns, Xperiment is about the curiosity that pushes us beyond what we already know. Join us on October 18th, 2026 at Pauley Ballroom as we ask new questions, test new possibilities, and see where they take us. Check out our speaker lineup at www.tedxberkeley.org.

events.description: The Department of Music holds an annual concerto audition in the fall semester, open to current members of the UC Berkeley Symphony Orchestraand to music majors performing on non-orchestral instruments (i.e. piano, voice, instruments from other cultures). Free and open to the publicInformation for Applicants: The deadline to submit application forms is Wednesday, November 6, 4pm in the Music Department office, 104 Morrison Hall. The application form can be found here(PDF file). Copies of the form are also available in 104 Morrison Hall. The audition jury is made up of Music Department faculty and outside professionals. Winner/s will be chosen to perform their concerto with the symphony, usually by the end of the next calendar school year.General audition rules:Applicants performing on standard orchestral instruments must be current members of the UC Berkeley Symphony Orchestra. The auditions are also open to Music majors who perform on non-orchestral instruments including piano, voice, guitar, instruments from other cultures, etc. Applicants must currently be studying privately with department faculty. Applicants may present excerpts of their choice (which should be representative of the whole work), but must be prepared to play any part of the entire work if asked to do so by the panel. Memorization is preferred but not mandatory. Lengthy extended orchestral tuttis should be omitted during the audition. The jury panel reserves the right to choose several winners or none. events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

events.title: Dreams' Navel: Revisiting a Bengali Modernist Classic Akhtaruzzaman Elias's Khwabnama
events.description: A panel discussion on Dreams' Navel: Revisiting a Bengali Modernist Classic—Akhtaruzzaman Elias's Khwabnama (https://uplbooks.com/shop/9789845067119-dreams-navel-23890?utm_source=chatgpt.com), a new volume edited by Firdous Azim (https://www.bracu.ac.bd/about/people/firdous-azim-phd?utm_source=chatgpt.com) and Naveeda Khan (https://anthropology.jhu.edu/directory/naveeda-khan/?utm_source=chatgpt.com). Bringing together the volume's editors and contributors, the panel will consider the enduring significance of Akhtaruzzaman Elias's landmark novel Khwabnama, exploring its distinctive engagement with history, memory, politics, and rural life in Bengal and its place in Bengali and global literary thought.Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies and Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley.PanelistsEditor: Firdous Azim (https://www.bracu.ac.bd/about/people/firdous-azim-phd?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Professor of English and Humanities at BRAC UniversityEditor: Naveeda Khan (https://anthropology.jhu.edu/directory/naveeda-khan/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Professor of Anthropology at Johns Hopkins UniversityNasrin Khandoker (https://juniv.edu/teachers/nasrin.khandoker?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Postdoctoral Fellow, University College CorkDina M. Siddiqi (https://liberalstudies.nyu.edu/about/faculty-listing/dina-siddiqi.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Clinical Professor in Liberal Studies at New York UniversityKamran Ali (https://experts.utexas.edu/kamran_ali?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Professor of Anthropology at the University of Texas at AustinHumayun Kabir (https://qc-undergraduate.catalog.cuny.edu/departments/PSCI-QC/faculty?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Adjunct Assistant Professor of Political Science at Queens College, CUNYNaeem Mohaiemen (https://arts.columbia.edu/profiles/naeem-mohaiemen?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Associate Professor of Visual Arts at Columbia University. _________________DATE: Mon, Oct 19, 2026 TIME: 9 am Berkeley | Calculate your local time (https://www.thetimezoneconverter.com/)ZOOM: Register HERE (https://berkeley.zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_h0uy7TJ1TZGt45ZkYO4k_w) _________________ This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter)_________________ ABOUT THE BOOKDreams' Navel (https://uplbooks.com/shop/9789845067119-dreams-navel-23890?utm_source=chatgpt.com) provides an interdisciplinary exploration of Akhtaruzzaman Elias's Khwabnama, a monumental work of Bengali modernist fiction. This collection of essays examines how the novel enriches official nationalist histories of Bangladesh and the 1947 Partition. By attending to the 'minutiae of locality'—the marshes, myths, and memories of rural North Bengal —contributors from anthropology, literature, and political science demonstrate Elias's unique ability to weave the oneiric and the magical into historical experience. The volume offers fresh reflections on subaltern agency, gendered domesticity, and the evocative sensory world of the Bengali rural landscape. Dreams' Navel provides a transformative vantage on a classic text, positioning Elias not just within the Bengali canon, but as a vital and provocative voice in global conceptual inquiry. This scholarly tribute is essential for readers seeking to understand the enduring power of Elias's literary imagination and its resonance in the postcolonial world. ABOUT THE EDITORSFirdous Azim is Professor of English at BRAC University in Dhaka, Bangladesh. She has published widely on literary, cultural and women's issues both inside and outside the country. Her critical writings include The Colonial Rise of the Novel (1993), as well as contributions on postcolonial and women's writings in journals and edited anthologies. She is a founding member of Naripokkho, a women's activist group in Bangladesh.Naveeda Khan is Professor of Anthropology at Johns Hopkins University, where she is affiliated with Women, Gender, Sexuality; Islamic Studies; Environmental Science and Studies; and the Department of Comparative Thought and Literature. Her publications include In Quest of a Shared Planet: Negotiating Climate from the Global South (2023), River Life and the Upspring of Nature (2022), and Muslim Becoming: Aspiration and Skepticism in Pakistan (2012). events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: The single-genaerator problem for $C^*$-algebras
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Chun Guang Li, Northeast Normal UniversityThe single-generator problem asks whether every simple separable $C^*$-algebra can be generated by a single element. It is closely related to the classical generator problem for von Neumann algebras. In this talk, I will first review the background and some of the main developments concerning this problem. I will then present recent joint work on several classes of $C^*$-algebras. we prove that each Villadsen algebra of the first type is singly generated. In contrast, we construct a Villadsen algebra of the second kind that is not singly generated. For crossed products, we prove that if σ is a minimal homeomorphism of a compact metrizable space $X$, then $C(X)times Z$ is singly generated. Finally, we establish that the reduced group $C^*$-algebra $C_r^*(F_2)$ of the free group on two generators is singly generated. The results presented in this talk arise from joint work, in different collaborations with George A. Elliott, Zhuang Niu and M. Ruzicka.

events.title: 10/19 TAC Seminar - Jonathan C. Tan (Chalmers / U. Virginia)
events.description: Title: The Origin of Supermassive Black Holes from Pop III.1 Seeds and Implications for Particle Physics and CosmologyAbstract: The origin of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) is a key open question for contemporary astrophysics and cosmology. I review various formation scenarios for SMBHs and then discuss the predictions of the Pop III.1 model, i.e., seeding via metal-free stars forming in locally isolated dark matter minihalos, where dark matter annihilation has a chance to alter the structure of the star allowing growth to supermassive scales (Banik, Tan & Monaco 2019; Singh, Monaco & Tan 2023; Cammelli et al. 2025; Sanati et al. 2025a,b; Nandal et al. 2026; for a review see Tan et al. 2024 and this project page: http://cosmicorigins.space/smbh (http://cosmicorigins.space/smbh)). The model predicts that all SMBHs form very early in the Universe (i.e., by z = 20) with a spatial distribution that is initially relatively unclustered. It also makes predictions for SMBH occupation fractions, host galaxy properties, frequency of binary SMBHs and the gravitational wave background. These predictions are compared to latest results from the Hubble Space Telescope, James Webb Spact Telescope and pulsar timing array observations. Another key prediction is an early phase of "flash" ionization of the universe at z~20, which can help alleviate cosmological tensions (Hubble tension, dynamical dark energy, negative neutrino masses) (Tan 2025; Tan & Komatsu 2026; Aggarwal et al. 2026). Finally, since the Pop III.1 mechanism relies on the process of WIMP dark matter self-annihilation, there are implication for the nature of the dark matter particle.Host: TBD

events.title: CSLS Speaker Series: When Federal Climate Policy Works: Benefits, Business, and Politics (The MIT Press, 2026)
events.organizer: Center for the Study of Law and Society
events.description: featuring David Vogel, Solomon P. Lee Chair Distinguished Professor Emeritus of Business Ethics and Professor Emeritus of Political Science, UC BerkeleyAbstract: When Federal Climate Policy Works challenges the widely accepted belief that the federal government has been unable to adopt effective policies to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Roger Karapin and David Vogel argue that the federal government has made measurable progress by adopting more narrowly focused sectoral policies. These have reduced GHG emissions in many sectors: through fuel economy and GHG standards for motor vehicles, the promotion of electric vehicles, mandatory standards and voluntary Energy Star labels for the energy efficiency of appliances and equipment, tax credits for renewable energy investments and production, restrictions on HFCs, and regulations on methane emissions from landfills and oil and gas production. Almost all of these measures began as unintentional climate policies during the 1970s, when they received substantial bipartisan support. Their initial policy frameworks have exhibited substantial continuity even after the policies become repositioned as more politically contentious, explicit climate change policies during the 1990s and later decades. Throughout the last 50 years, policy adoption has depended on including non-climate benefits, gaining business acceptance, and navigating partisan politics.
