events.title: Neyman Statistics Seminar with Reese Pathak: Revisiting statistical principles for risk minimization
events.description: Abstract: Minimizing a loss over a set of data points is ubiquitous in data science. A complete understanding of which loss to minimize, however, is lacking. This talk focuses on an extremely simple model: estimating an unknown mean corrupted by Gaussian noise. An intuitive guess is that minimizing square loss (equivalently, maximizing the likelihood) over the parameter space would be the best estimator possible. Counterintuitively, this is suboptimal in general. Embarrassingly, the reasons for why this occurs are not fully understood! I will explain some reasons why this can happen, what can be done about it, and some related results around this theme. Based on several papers, joint with Liviu Aoloritei (UC Berkeley), Cong Ma (U. Chicago), Michael I. Jordan (UC Berkeley/INRIA), Annie Ulichney (UC Berkeley), and Nikita Zhivotovskiy (UC Berkeley).

events.title: Close Reading in the Wake of Philology | A talk by Prof. Frances Ferguson
events.location: Wheeler Hall, Room 315, Maude Fife Room
events.description: John Guillory's brief book On Close Reading has focused attention on the centrality of exercises in close reading to literary studies in English. Ferguson will be tracking his argument that close reading has no ideological entailments and will follow his example of focusing attention on W.K. Wimsatt's own questions about close reading, which Wimsatt calls criticism by explication. Ferguson will conclude by examining two of Wimsatt's essays as instances of close reading that inflect his famous doctrinal statements on intention and affect. Before retiring from the University of Chicago as the Mabel Greene Myers Distinguished Service Professor of English in 2023, Frances Ferguson taught at Johns Hopkins University (1973-77), UC-Berkeley (1977-1988), Johns Hopkins (1988-2004; 2005-2012) and the University of Chicago (2004-05, 2012-2023). She has recently published a selection of essays, Records of Reward: Essays on Literature and Value, with a Foreward by Wendy A. Lee and a conversation with Nate Crocker. Earlier work includes Wordsworth: Language as Counter-Spirit, Solitude and the Sublime: Romanticism and the Aesthetics of Individuation; and Pornography, The Theory: What Utilitarianism Did To Action. Please note we will also gather for lunch and in conversation with Professor Ferguson on Samuel Richardson's Clarissa on Thursday, Oct. 22, from 12-1:30 pm in the Wheeler Hall Lounge (Room 330).

events.description: The Garden is honored to host author, educator, and curator Dr. Giovanni Aloi, whose work focuses on the representation of nature and the environment in art. Aloi has published numerous books, including Botanical Revolutions (2025), and is the founder and editor-in-chief of Antennae: The Journal of Nature in Visual Culture. For this talk co-sponsored by Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative and Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archives, Aloi follows the making of the artist myth, as explored in his most recent book I'm Not an Artist (2025), and proposes an eco-cultural model for artistic life.About the TalkNew Art Eco-models: Reclaiming Creativity in the Age of Infinite Content In this lecture, Giovanni Aloi follows the making of the artist myth, from the Renaissance master to the modern rebel and creative entrepreneur, exposing institutions, wealth, and exclusions that have sustained it. Against this exhausted genealogy, his book I'm Not an Artist (2025) proposes an eco-cultural model for artistic life. Creativity precedes art. It exceeds galleries and markets, emerging as a generative force through which living beings continually reshape their worlds. Seen ecologically, the artist can no longer be imagined as an isolated genius. The artist becomes an organism among organisms, entangled with collaborators, audiences, materials, economies, and more-than-human agencies. From this perspective, the art world itself begins to resemble a habitat: diverse, interdependent, sustained through exchanges whose value cannot always be measured. How can ecologically minded artists lead the way to a complete reconsideration of the art world and the future of creativity? —About the Presenter Dr. Giovanni Aloi is an author, educator, and curator whose work focuses on the representation of nature and the environment in art. Aloi is the editor-in-chief of Antennae: The Journal of Nature in Visual Culture and editor of the University of Minnesota Press series 'Art after Nature'. He has written and edited numerous books on the representation of the natural world, with a particular focus on vegetal imagery, including Why Look at Plants? (2018), Botanical Revolutions (2025), and Lawn (2025). He has collaborated with institutions such as the BBC, PBS, Whitechapel Gallery, Tate, and the Art Institute of Chicago, and has curated exhibitions across the United States and Europe.Special Acknowledgement Special thanks to Shirley Watts of Natural Discourse for connecting us with our presenter. —Event Details Reception: 4:30 PM Lecture: 5 PM Garden admission included (collections close at 5:00 PM)Transportation and Parking UC Berkeley students and affiliates are encouraged to utilize the campus Hill shuttle (https://pt.berkeley.edu/public-transportation/bear-transi), which leaves every 30 minutes from Hearst Mining Circle. See the schedule here (https://pt.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/2025-10-09_h_line_timetable.pdf). Parking is available at the Garden at $1.50/hr at the pay machine.

events.title: Blaise Agüera y Arcas: What Is Intelligence?
events.location: Calvin Lab Auditorium, Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing
events.description: To many AI researchers it came as a surprise that a large neural network trained only to predict the next word can show signs of general intelligence. Neuroscientists who hold the "predictive brain" hypothesis — that brains evolved above all to anticipate the future — were less surprised. In this talk, based on his book of the same title, Blaise Agüera y Arcas takes this idea further and argues that prediction is fundamental not just to brains but to life itself. He offers a broad picture of intelligence that runs from molecules to organisms, societies, and AI, drawing on computer science, biology, physics, and neuroscience.

events.title: Kimberly Garza & Erik Prince: Small Moves, Meaningful Change | Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning Lecture
events.description: Join us for an evening with Lifchez Professors of Practice in Social Justice Kimberly Garza (BA Landscape Architecture 2006) and Erik Prince, principals of Atlas Lab, a mission-driven landscape architecture, urban design, and public art practice. Through a series of research initiatives and built projects, this lecture explores the role of the designer as an instigator, storyteller, and builder of conscious change in cities. About Kimberly Garza (https://ced.berkeley.edu/people/kimberly-garza) is principal of Atlas Lab Inc., a woman- and minority-owned, mission-driven landscape architecture, urban design, and public art studio. With a steadfast commitment to effecting conscious change in the built environment, Garza spearheads initiatives that foster accessible, positive, and progressive impacts on communities. With 20 years of experience in the field, Garza is a seasoned landscape architect, artist, educator, and keynote speaker. Her portfolio spans private and public developments nationwide, with her work being internationally recognized, published, and exhibited. Garza's dedication to innovation and leadership has earned her accolades, including being named the 2023–2024 Landscape Architecture Foundation Fellow for Innovation and Leadership, as well as being recognized as a 40 Under 40 Urban Innovator by NextCity.org and a 40 Under 40 Honoree by the Sacramento Business Journal. She holds a bachelor of arts in landscape architecture from UC Berkeley and a Master of Landscape Architecture from the Harvard Graduate School of Design. Erik Prince (https://ced.berkeley.edu/people/erik-prince) is a principal at Atlas Lab, Inc., a woman- and minority-owned, mission-driven landscape architecture, urban design, and public art studio. Prince shapes the firm's approach to culturally and ecologically responsive design. His work translates regional narratives into layered, sensory experiences, revealing how movement, memory, and cultural history shape the ways people inhabit and perceive place. Prince's work spans resilient planning, urban parks, public landscapes, and art installations. His experience includes the Grand Bayway for the Resilient by Design Bay Area Challenge, Boulder Civic Area, and numerous public art projects that explore innovative fabrication and material expression. At Atlas Lab, he has guided major projects including the River District Strategic Plan, Mill Street Pedestrian Plaza, Sacramento Waterfront, and Capitol Mall, reimagining streets and public spaces as social, restorative, and climate-responsive landscapes. Prince holds a BS in landscape architecture from Colorado State University and a Master of Landscape Architecture from the Harvard Graduate School of Design, where he graduated with distinction and received the Jacob Weidenmann Prize, the Department of Landscape Architecture's highest award for design. This lecture is sponsored by the Department of Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning.

events.title: Film Screening: Marjorie Keller Films
events.description: A key figure of American experimental film from the 1970s until her untimely death in 1994, filmmaker, scholar, activist, and teacher Marjorie Keller redefined Stan Brakhage's approach to personal, handmade films in feminist terms. Keller's subjects ranged from social and political critiques to intimate portraits of people who populated her world, and her intricate visual and sound editing is pointed while also being poetically suggestive. Following the release of Daughters of Chaos in 1980, critic Amy Taubin wrote, "Its central concern is female bonding . . . Keller's strongest gifts as a filmmaker (are) the subtlety of her awareness of gesture and the extraordinary fluidity and assurance of her editing."

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. events.title: Global Diversification of Tropical Rain Forests: from Herbaria to Spectra
events.description: Tropical rain forests are the most diverse ecosystems on Earth. How this extraordinary diversity arose remains one of evolutionary biology's enduring questions. I will present results from a global study of Annonaceae, a pantropical plant family of about 2,500 species, as a window into rain forest evolution.At the heart of our approach is the herbarium specimen, from which we extracted DNA, morphology, distribution data and spectra. Our near-complete phylogenomic tree, covering 82% of species, 65% from herbarium specimens, and interpreted with fossil evidence, reveals a more dynamic history than expected, with waxing and waning of diversity over the past 90 million years.To explain present-day diversity, we analyzed more than 100 environmental and evolutionary variables, identifying large regions, even across continents, where similar processes shape diversity. We also show that future extinctions would have a decoupled impact on phylogenetic and functional diversity across the family. Near-infrared spectroscopy now extends what a specimen can tell us, offering a rapid, non-destructive way, to identify specimens and to prioritize them for genomic work.Finally, I will briefly show how these global patterns can guide local action, through a community-based forest conservation partnership in Ecuador. Herbaria are not only archives of the past, but living infrastructures for understanding, and helping to conserve biodiversity.

events.description: In July 2025, the International Court of Justice issued its landmark advisory opinion on states' obligations in respect of climate change. Albert wrote a 2026 UN University paper on what the opinion means for future generations. RSVP here. events.title: Critical Foundations: Sociology of Law
events.description: The criminal legal system we confront today is the product of nearly 1000 years of development during which new institutions, new powers, and new myths about crime and punishment have been installed in response to periodic crises originating in the political and economic conflicts of society. The result is a kind of carceral leviathan that can appear in many ways to suit the needs of the time and overcome moral and practical criticisms.In the lecture, Professor Simon will review this history and how it continues to be relevant today to those seeking to reform or even abolish it.Jonathan Simon graduated from Berkeley law with a JD and a PhD in the Jurisprudence and Social Policy program. Simon is the author of three books and many articles on the criminal legal system in the United States and its relationship to shifts in American society and democracy.He has been a professor at Berkeley Law since 2003.Lunch will be served inside of Room 170 starting at 12:50 PM. events.title: Lecture | Order of Debt: Power, Wealth, and Death in the Ottoman Empire, 1700–1830
events.description: This talk investigates the relationship between property, capital, finance, and Ottoman statehood in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. It examines the political and financial actors who shaped the accumulation of wealth and power, tracing public and private debts, networks of obligation, and the making of state order between roughly 1700 and 1830. Drawing on Ottoman fiscal records as well as probate and debt inventories that employ distinctive accounting techniques, the talk shows how postmortem estate settlement became a key site where sovereignty, credit, and coercion intersected.Bio: Dr. Ali Yaycıoğlu is Associate Professor of History at Stanford University and a historian of the Ottoman Empire and modern Turkey whose work examines political economy, law, and state–society relations from the early modern to the modern period. He is the author of Partners of the Empire: Crisis of the Ottoman Order in the Age of Revolutions (2016) and is completing The Order of Debt: Power, Wealth, and Death in the Ottoman Empire. He directs Stanford's digital history lab, Charting the Empire, which develops tools and data for working with Ottoman fiscal codices and distinctive accounting techniques. His essays on democracy, capitalism, and populism in Turkey appear in Uncertain Past Time: Empire, Republic, and Politics (Istanbul, 2024, in Turkish).

events.title: Astronomy Colloquium - Malena Rice (Yale)
events.description: Title: Dynamical Demographics of Exoplanet SystemsAbstract: The census of confirmed exoplanets has grown to the thousands, with nearly all known systems demonstrating fundamental properties distinct from those of the solar system. We have entered an era of population-level planetary system characterization—yet the demographics of planetary systems are not static. Instead, they are subject to dynamic processes that shape orbital distributions across systems' full life cycles, with clues to the prevalence and diversity of these processes encoded in exoplanets' observed orbital configurations. In this talk, I will share recent advances in our understanding of 3D orbital architectures across classes of exoplanet systems. I will discuss the relationship between modern observational constraints and theoretical implications for exoplanet-hosting single-star and binary star systems, as well as prospects for future advancements with ground- and space-based surveys.Host: Eugene Chiang

events.title: Subhrajit Guhathakurta: Hurricanes, Flooding, and Displacement — AI-Accelerated Flood Risk Mapping and Human Relocation Dynamics | City & Regional Planning Lecture
events.description: Hydrodynamic models are essential for understanding flood processes, but their computational demands limit their use for updating flood risk during rapidly evolving storm conditions. Subhrajit "Subhro" Guhathakurta presents an alternative approach that combines crowdsourced information with a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) to generate full-field, near-real-time flood risk maps with modest computational requirements. This approach is validated in a testbed in Pinellas County, Florida, through a series of fixed cameras that capture and transmit images at 15-minute intervals. In the second part of the talk, Guhathakurta discusses the consequences of flooding from natural hazards on people's intention to relocate and, if they do, their destination choices using mobile GPS-based mobility data. Finally, he discusses the generalizability of these findings and their impacts on housing markets. About Subhrajit "Subhro" Guhathakurta is the Harry West Chair Professor at Georgia Tech's School of City and Regional Planning, where he directs the Center for Urban Resilience and Analytics and the Urban Analytics master's program. Formerly the school's chair, he also held leadership and faculty roles at Arizona State University's School of Sustainability and School of Geographical Sciences and Urban Planning. Guhathakurta has published extensively on urban heat, energy systems, sustainable development, active transportation, and geospatial technologies. His editorial contributions include co-editing the Journal of Planning Education and Research and serving as associate editor for the Journal of the American Planning Association. He is a recipient of the Chester Rapkin Award and the Mercator Professorship. He has held visiting appointments in the UK, Germany, India, Australia, Sweden, and China, and continues to work with several scholars worldwide. This lecture is part of the Department of City & Regional Planning's fall lecture series.

events.title: (Screening) Omar Khan | Mohenjo Daro: Unsealing an Ancient Indus City.
events.description: Join us for a screening of Mohenjo-daro: Unsealing an Ancient Indus Cit (https://www.harappa.com/video/mohenjo-daro-unsealing-ancient-indus-city)y, a documentary that explores one of the world's greatest lost civilizations — the Indus Valley Civilization – through the eyes of Omar Khan, the founder of Harappa.com. Screening with filmmaker, Omar Khan present. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, October 22, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: On FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ———���—-About the Film: Omar Khan walks through the nearly five thousand year old city of Mohenjo-daro, discusses recent speculations about the Great Bath and the so-called Stupa mound, and raises many unanswered questions about this Bronze Age civilization while sharing recent perspectives and information. High quality graphics, countless actual Indus seals, pottery and sculptures photographed by leading archaeologists like Drs. Jonathan Mark Kenoyer and Richard H. Meadow; new photography and rare archival images from the earliest excavators; a handful of key recreations of the Great Bath and Stupa-Mound; the voices and music of Sindh from premiere music studio Lahooti Live Sessions. Featuring interviews with leading scholars, this film is ideal for students, educators, and anyone curious about the ancient world and the Indus civilization, the original urban civilization which some 2 billion people can claim descent from in modern India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. The documentary is divided into five chapters: 1. The Story, 2. The City, 3. The Citadel, 4. The Writing and 5. The Future. Includes the voices and opinions of Dr. Ahmad Hasan Dani, Dr. Romila Thapar, Dr. Shereen Ratnagar, Dr. Ghulam Mustafa Shar, Iravatham Mahadevan, Sheikh Javid Ali Sindhi, Irshad Ali Solangi and Mohammad Ilyas. Running time 37 minutes. See the trailer HERE (https://vimeo.com/1215616294/b822951167). He has researched early photography and ephemera of the subcontinent for thirty years and collects the early postcards featured here. He is an avid historian and award-winning web designer. Omar Khan's previous book is From Kashmir to Kabul: The Photographs of John Burke and William Baker 1860-1900 (http://www.kashmirtokabul.com/) (Prestel/Gallimard/Mapin, 2002). He has run the website Harappa.com (https://www.harappa.com/) since 1995, and recently retired as Chief Technology Officer (CTO) at Common Sense Media (https://www.commonsensemedia.org/) in San Francisco, California where he lives. events.title: Visiting Artist Lecture Series: Zeina Barakeh
events.location: Anthropology and Art Practice Building, Room 285
events.description: The Department of Art Practice is excited to welcome Zeina Barakeh for our Fall '26 Visiting Artist Lecture Series. This lecture will take place from 5-6:30pm in Room 285, Anthropology and Art Practice Building (AAPB). All artist talks are free and open to the public. "CYBOTAGE: Brain-Computer Interfaces and the Politics of Public Art" In this talk, Zeina Barakeh will map the trajectory of her work from gallery and museum contexts into public art, using research to lodge her practice within—and against—the infrastructures and ethics of global security. Her project CYBOTAGE—an ongoing investigation into brain–computer interfaces and military human enhancement—extends across public works, workshops with veterans, webinars, and research as artistic intervention. Zeina Barakeh (b. Beirut) is a Palestinian Lebanese artist whose work is shaped by lived experience in wartime Lebanon. She examines the militarization of the body, surveillance, human enhancement, and the shifting boundaries between humans and machines across kinetic and cyberwarfare. Her public art works include Standard of Capital for the Salesforce Tower Top (San Francisco); PsyClone Calafia, commissioned by the San Francisco Arts Commission; Remix on the ZAZ Corner Jumbotron (Times Square); and CYBOGUARDIANS on the MIX Center façade (Mesa, Arizona). Exhibitions span MuCEM (Marseille); Yinchuan MOCA (China); the Asian Art Museum (San Francisco); Peabody Essex Museum (Salem); Catharine Clark Gallery (San Francisco); Bernstein Gallery at Princeton University; and the Middle East Institute (Washington, DC), among others. Her film festivals include the 11th Harlem International Film Festival (New York), the 19th Kerry Film Festival (Ireland), the Female Filmmakers Festival Berlin, and the Los Angeles Art-House Film Festival, where her work has received awards for experimental animation. She has held residencies at the Brodsky Center for Innovative Editions and the Vermont Studio Center. Barakeh is the recipient of the 2024 SF Bay Area Artadia Award and the 2025 Leonardo-ASU Seed Grant for CYBOTAGE.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

events.title: Symposium: Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: Morrison Library & Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley
events.description: In the spring of 1985, thousands of UC Berkeley students took to Sproul Plaza to demand the University divest from companies doing business in apartheid South Africa—the culmination of over a decade of organizing. Backed by faculty and staff, and particularly inspired by the bold actions of Bay Area labor unions, the movement shaped a generation of activists and connected UC Berkeley to the broader global struggle against apartheid. Featuring Jeff Chang, Pedro Noguera, Andrea Prichett (panelists), and Rickey Vincent (tour leader) —students who were directly involved in the movement—the symposium will feature a panel discussion, collection viewing, and tours to create space to explore the stories, complexities, and nuances behind the anti-apartheid movement. This event is free and open to the public. The panel discussion will be recorded. This event is organized by The Bancroft Library, African American & African Diaspora Studies, and Ethnic Studies. This event is co-sponsored by the American Cultures Center, Asian American Research Center, the Office of the President of the Associated Students of the University of California (ASUC), the Center for African Studies, the Othering & Belonging Institute, the Institute for the Study of Societal Issues, the Mellon Foundation's Affirming Multivocal Humanities Funds for Ethnic Studies, Palestinian & Arab Studies Program, and the Center for Race and Gender at UC Berkeley.

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Dr. Vivek Singh, NVIDIA | Let's Talk About the Good: How AI and AC are Enabling Semiconductor Scaling
events.description: Abstract: There is no arguing that advancements in semiconductor technology have improved the lives of billions of human beings around the world for the past half century. One would like to continue these improvements but chip manufacturing gets harder every year, and fundamental physics appears to inhibit our desire for continued scaling. The solutions to this problem increasingly involve more precise modeling and intricate optimization strategies, across multiple modules in the Fab. It is clear that if there is a "law" that governs the annual increase in Fab computation, it has an exponent greater than Moore's Law ever did. Accelerated Computing (AC) helps solve this problem by drastically reducing the cost and energy required for these computations, thereby making possible previously prohibitive techniques and precision. On top of that, Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods, with their increasing ability to describe the physical world, have started to prove themselves in real world situations. This talk will describe the problem, some solutions, and give examples of how AC and AI are moving into production in advanced Fabs. Bio: Dr. Vivek Singh is vice president in the Advanced Technology Group at NVIDIA, working on computational methods for advanced silicon manufacturing. He was previously an Intel Fellow and director of the Computational Imaging Department, where he led the development and deployment of software platforms at scale, providing industry-first solutions in the domains of diffractive optics, microscopic inspection and chip design. Vivek's been an SPIE Fellow since 2012. He has served as president of the Lithography Workshop, as honorary visiting professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi, and as founding member and chair of the Design Technology Co-Optimization conference in SPIE. Vivek has a B.Tech. from IIT Delhi and an M.S. and Ph.D. from Stanford University.

events.title: Group Actions and Dynamics Seminar: Winning of badly approximable vectors on manifolds
events.description: Speaker: Liyang Shao, BerkeleyDiophantine approximation, the study of approximating vectors by rationals, has long been connected to homogeneous dynamics thanks to Dani. In particular, badly approximable vectors are an interesting object to study due to its smallness in Lebesgue measure, and yet largeness in Hausdorff dimension. In this talk, we will first introduce Dani's correspondence. Then we will recall how nondivergence estimates from Kleinbock-Margulis can be applied to show the winning property(stronger than full Hausdorff dimension) of badly approximable vectors, in terms of the game first introduced by Schmidt. If time permits, we will go into details about the difficulty of such application on manifolds and how it can be resolved. This is joint work with Shreyasi Datta.

events.title: Indispensable but Invisible: Legal Expertise and Juridical Capital in the Governance of Late Imperial China | Lecture by Li Chen
events.description: During the Qing period (1644–1912), late imperial China was in theory governed by approximately two thousand local administrators who were appointed for their mastery of the Confucian classics rather than for their administrative or legal expertise. How did these scholar-officials actually carry out the daily tasks of local governance, including judicial administration? Based on a forthcoming monograph, this talk analyzes the training and roles of the thousands of legal specialists who advised local officials behind the scenes and handled most of the judicial and other substantive administrative work on their behalf. Despite their important functions in local governance, these legal specialists were ideologically marginalized. This talk, as well as the larger study from which it is drawn, provides new insights into why they became so indispensable to Qing law and governance and why they remained obscure to outsiders and modern researchers. Speaker BioLi Chen, J.D. (UIUC) and Ph.D. (Columbia), is Professor of History at the University of Toronto, with a cross-appointment at the Faculty of Law. Among his extensive publications on the intersection of law, culture, and politics in Chinese and international history since the 1500s is his monograph,Chinese Law in Imperial Eyes: Sovereignty, Justice, and Transcultural Politics(Columbia University Press, 2016), which received the 2018 Joseph Levenson Book Prize from the Association for Asian Studies and an Honorable Mention for the 2017 Peter Gonville Stein Book Award from the American Society for Legal History. He has recently completed another monograph,Invisible Power in China: Legal Expertise, Statecraft Traditions, and Cultural Politics, 1651–1911. He was the founding president (2014–2017) of the International Society for Chinese Law and History and currently serves on the boards of that organization and the American Society for Legal History. He also serves on the editorial boards ofLaw and History Review,Law & Social Inquiry, and theJournal of World History. He is currently working on book projects on the Qing system of Autumn Assizes for major criminal cases and on the remarkable but little-known history of Qing legal lineages.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Brandon Barnett, Assistant Professor, University of RochesterNon-Heme Iron Enzyme Mimicry Through Confinement Biological enzymes have evolved over billions of years to mediate kinetically challenging transformations under mild conditions and with excellent selectivities. Inspired by nature, our group works at the interface of bioinorganic chemistry and materials science toward the precise engineering of void spaces that can kinetically stabilize high-valent, bio-inspired complexes. This talk will focus principally on the chemistry of bio-inspired high-valent iron-oxo and iron-nitrosyl species that have been kinetically stabilized through confinement within a rigid macrocycle. The unique thermal stabilities of these species enable novel investigations of their photochemical behaviors both in solution and in the solid state. Most notably, photocrystallographic studies have illuminated novel C–C cleavage reactions mediated by "oxyl"-type excited states of a confined high-spin iron(IV)-oxo. Mechanistic studies of reactions arising from direct photoexcitation of this complex will be discussed. At the end of the talk, I will briefly highlight our work using dynamic porous solids for separation science and energy storage.The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.title: Music Studies Colloquium: Rachana Vajjhala (University of California, Davis)
events.description: Thinking Through NautchworkRachana Vajjhala (University of California, Davis) In this talk, I share two threads of my current book project. The first considers Indianist danced works at the turn of the twentieth century, with a focus on Le Dieu bleu (1912). Rather than characteristic Russian locales or reimagined Hellenic ones, this ballet was set in a mythologized version of the subcontinent. In the words of a critic for Revue hebdomadaire, there was a chasm between "the strongly colored gestural aspect of Le Dieu bleu and the lightly shaded musical one." Registral discordances were nothing new for such productions of course, but I dwell here on the coloristic language, which was both literal and metaphorical. Nijinska shaded her body with makeup and darkly hued tights, but Nijinsky blued his skin from head to toe. In this way, Le Dieu bleu anticipates a more complexly tinted approach to Indianist markers of performed authenticity to come. The rest of my talk picks up another strand of Nautchwork, specifically the way earlier danced productions (including Le Dieu bleu) contributed to the aestheticization of a contiguous embodied practice—postural yoga—as well as the shift of those Indianist markers from a visual dimension to the sonic register of the teacher's voice. Rachana Vajjhala is an Assistant Professor of Musicology at UC Davis. Her first book, Kinetic Cultures, was published by UC Press in 2024. A reception will follow.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

events.title: Film Screening: La maison des bois: Episodes 4–7
events.description: Epic yet intimate, sweeping yet personal, La maison des bois stands as one of the greatest achievements in the history of television, as well as legendary director Maurice Pialat's magnum opus. Commissioned for Télévision Française in 1971, this seven-episode, nearly four-hundred-minute miniseries considers the impact of World War I on a simple French family living in the countryside. Applying a naturalistic focus to their subject, Pialat and screenwriter René Wheeler capture both the historical scope of the conflict and the subtle ways that a small town's quotidian routines and rituals—church, school, tavern—are indelibly touched by it.

events.title: Film Screening: Le petit soldat
events.description: Leave it to Jean-Luc Godard to create a spy/terrorist "hero" who'd rather moon over a woman's eyes ("Were they Velazquez gray or Renoir gray?") than fight. Disillusioned and in love with himself above all, young Bruno is a French spy (or counterspy, or something) in neutral Geneva during the French-Algerian War, blithely taking hit orders from his superiors. Meeting the gray-eyed Veronica turns his mind further away from politics (she is Anna Karina, after all, in her first Godard role), but her involvement in an Algerian revolutionary group quickly has him running not just from the torturers on the "other side," but also from his own supposed allies.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Vidrine- Worth Ryder Galler, Anthropology & Art Practice Building
events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra seminar: Traces on Weak Lorentz Ideals and Nonclassical Weyl Laws
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote online talk
events.description: Speaker: Raphael Ponge, University of OttawaIn Connes' noncommutative geometry, traces on operator ideals play the role of the integral. The basic examples are Dixmier traces and, more generally, positive normalized traces on the weak trace class $L_{1,\infty }$. This setting is taylored to classical Weyl laws, where eigenvalues decay like $j^{-1/p}$. Many natural operators, however, obey nonclassical Weyl laws with logarithmic corrections, $\lambda _j\sim c, j^{-1/p}(\log j)^q$. Examoles include Dirichlet Laplacians on infinite-volume domains, Dirac operators on open manifolds with cusps and assuming the Riemann Hypothesis, the Dirac operator of Connes–Moscovici whose eigenvalues are the imaginary parts of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Such operators lie outside$L_{1,\infty }$, in weak Lorentz ideals associated with regularly varying functions. This talk is about traces on these ideals. I will first show that an asymptotic additivity property for eigenvalue partial sums allows us to define Dixmier traces directly in terms of eigenvalue sequences. This leads to a spectral characterization of operators on which all Dixmier traces agree, answeing a question of Connes in this setting. I will then go beyond Dixmier traces and consider the whole class of positive normalized traces. The main tool is an extension of Pietsch's correspondence which relates traces on weak Lorentz ideals to invariant functionals on sequence spaces and places Dixmier traces within a broader picture. It yields a spectral characterization of operators on which all postive normalized traces agree. This extends results of Pietsch and Semenov–Sukochev–Usachev–Zanin for$L_{1,\infty }$. Combined with an extension of the Birman–Solomyak perturbation theory, it shows that operators satisfying Weyl laws take the same value on all positive normalized traces. I will also discuss a further notion, hypermeasurability. Finally, I will illustrate these results with examples, including the Riemann Hypothesis, the logarithm of th Laplacian, and products of Laplacians. This is joint work with Yongqiang Tian (Central South Univesity, Changsha, China).

events.title: North: The Future of Post-Climate America
events.description: With Jesse M. Keenan, Associate Professor of Sustainable Real Estate and Urban Planning, and Director, Center on Climate Change and Urbanism, Tulane University Climate change is already influencing how and where people live. Join us at BESI as urban planner Jesse M. Keenan discusses his new book, North: The Future of Post-Climate America, which explores how climate change is shaping the physical and demographic future of the United States. The book documents a new era marked by shifts in population that are transforming everything from the physical landscape of cities to electoral politics. At the dawning of this era, new geographies of risk and opportunity are resulting from physical climate impacts and the adaptations of market economies. Keenan reframes how people, markets, and public institutions shape human mobility and analyzes the capacity of American communities to adapt. With fast-moving markets and slow-moving governments, everyday people are caught in the crosshairs. While some will seek to preserve the status quo, others will relocate from places that are increasingly uninhabitable, too risky, or too expensive for permanent settlement. As the era of Sun Belt migration comes to an end and climate impacts accelerate, everything from local relocations to transcontinental climate migrations are already well underway. At the same time, new geographies of opportunity are receiving zones for those seeking a more sustainable and less precarious way of life. North is more than a collection of scientific observations and projections about America's future in the face of climate change. It's a projection of optimism about America's capacity for decarbonization, environmental stewardship, and population mobility.Register Now (https://forms.gle/ctEdNiGCNSjsSivB6) About the speaker Jesse M. Keenan is the Favrot II Associate Professor of Sustainable Real Estate and Urban Planning and the director of the Center on Climate Change and Urbanism at Tulane University. Keenan's research focuses on the intersection of climate change adaptation and the built environment, including aspects of applied science, design, regulation, and planning. Keenan has previously advised agencies of the U.S. government, governors, mayors, Fortune 500 companies, technology ventures, community enterprises, and international NGOs. Keenan previously served as the director and area head for Real Estate and the Built Environment program on the faculty of the Harvard Graduate School of Design and as the research director of the Center for Urban Real Estate on the faculty of the Graduate School of Architecture, Planning and Preservation at Columbia University.

events.title: CSLS Speaker Series: Terror on Trial: An Ethnography of French Courts (Cambridge University Press, 2026)
events.organizer: Center for the Study of Law and Society
events.description: featuring Sharon Weill, Professor of International Law and Director of the Justice Lab, The American University of ParisAbstract: Grounded in court ethnography, this book explores terrorism trials in France. A multidisciplinary research team examines how terrorism logics are reflected, represented, and negotiated within criminal proceedings. Based on hundreds of hearing days – ranging from small terrorism criminal cases to the so-called trials for history, commonly known as the 'Charlie Hebdo' and the 'Bataclan' trials – this study offers a nuanced, bottom-up perspective on the role of courts. Through courtroom immersion, close observation of legal performances, and interviews with judicial actors, it investigates how justice is shaped in practice. Identifying three generations of trials, the book provides original insights into the evolving role of courts in terrorism cases. From an empirical and comparative perspective, it also seeks to make criminal trials of civil law systems more accessible to Anglophone readers, offering a deeper understanding of how terrorism is prosecuted in France, highlighting the role of judges, prosecutors, lawyers, and victims.

events.title: From Limit Theorems to Finite-System Guarantees: Stein's Method for Stochastic Systems (Siva Theja, Georgia Tech)
events.description: Title: From Limit Theorems to Finite-System Guarantees: Stein's Method for Stochastic Systems Abstract: Limit theorems such as the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) form the foundation of probability theory, and have been used to study a variety of engineering systems. While these results completely characterize the behavior in the appropriate limit, they do not provide any guarantee on the prelimit system. Modern applications of stochastic systems in contrast, ask for guarantees on the finite i.e., nonasymptotic system. While some classical results such as the Chernoff or Hoeffding bound provide nonasymptotic guarantees, they are not tight asymptotically, i.e., they do not recover the limit theorems such as the CLT. The goal of our ongoing work is to develop results that are best of both worlds, i.e., nonasymptotic results that recover the limit theorems. One of the tools that enables one to obtain such results is the Stein's method. We present two vignettes of such sharp results obtained using the Stein's method, from two very different domains, viz., Stochastic Approximation and Stochastic Networks. The first one considers Stochastic Approximation that underlies today's machine learning algorithms including Reinforcement learning. The appropriately scaled iterates are known to converge to a Gaussian, and we establish the rate of convergence in the Wasserstein distance. We also provide prelimit tail bounds. The second vignette is a load balancing system in data centers consisting of queues where jobs are allowed to abandon. We study this system in the overloaded regime where a limit theorem converging to a Gaussian is known in the literature. We present efficient concentration, i.e., prelimit subGaussian tail bounds that recover the exact Gaussian in the limit. The talk concludes with a very brief overview of Stein's method that enables us to obtain these results. Bio: Siva Theja Maguluri is Fouts Family Early Career Professor and an Associate Professor in the H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering at Georgia Tech. He obtained his Ph.D. and MS in ECE as well as MS in Applied Math from UIUC, and B.Tech in Electrical Engineering from IIT Madras. His research interests span the areas of Control, Optimization, Algorithms and Applied Probability. In particular, he works on Reinforcement Learning theory, scheduling, resource allocation and revenue optimization problems that arise in a variety of systems. His research and teaching are recognized through several awards including the "Best Publication in Applied Probability" award, NSF CAREER award, second place award at INFORMS JFIG best paper competition, Student best paper award at IFIP Performance, "CTL/BP Junior Faculty Teaching Excellence Award," and "Student Recognition of Excellence in Teaching: Class of 1934 CIOS Award."

events.title: Julia Mahamid (Kuggie-Vallee Lecture): "In-cell structural biology at a systems level"
events.description: Kuggie-Vallee Lecture: (https://thevalleefoundation.org/programs/kdl) Recent technological breakthroughs in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) open the disruptive possibility to image macromolecular complexes in their native cellular or multicellular context at close to atomic resolution, and can directly reveal how their different conformational states and interaction networks are linked to biological functions. We advance sample preparation techniques for in-cell cryo-ET, including cryo-focused ion beam thinning and 3D correlative (super resolution) fluorescence microscopy. Preparations of such site-specific 'electron-transparent windows' enable the assignment of macromolecular structures directly from the high-resolution three-dimensional stills captured by cryo-ET when aided by an array of methods, including computational patter recognition and novel developments of genetically-encoded molecular tags. Furthermore, integration of multiple data sources is key to the interpretation of the mined structural signatures. For example, using the genome-reduced human pathogen Mycoplasma pneumoniae as a minimal cell model, we established the synergistic application of whole-cell crosslinking mass spectrometry and cellular cryo-ET to determine an in-cell integrative structural model of actively transcribing RNA polymerases coupled to translating ribosomes. Our contributions to computational methods now allow resolving these molecular machines to high resolution, reveal small molecule antibiotics bound to their active site in ribosomes within the intact pathogen, provide snapshots of their structural dynamics, and illuminate functions of previously unknown macromolecular complexes. Such integration of cutting-edge methods unlocks an enormous potential for mechanistic understanding at a system-spanning level by in-cell structural biology.

events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light'sBRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. events.title: Transportation Planning Fundamentals for California Streets
events.description: Description In today's environment, local streets and roads need to be planned, designed, built or retrofitted, operated, and maintained to provide safe, comfortable, and environmentally sustainable travel for all users of all ages and differing levels of mobility. Ideally these local streets and roads should provide for all modes, including walking, bicycling, taking transit, and driving. Local streets and roads must be operationally functional to allow for emergency response, road maintenance, and overall truck movement of goods. This course covers the planning and conceptual design of sustainable, multimodal, local streets and roads; the history of multimodal surface transportation planning in the US; the policy environment for sustainable, multimodal transportation; how to integrate multimodal transportation into the local urban planning process; and how to design local streets, intersections, crossings, and interchanges consistent with the sustainable, multimodal approach. The course's discussion of the legislative environment is focused on California. The course spans the full range of key areas from characteristics of the local roadway system, analysis of flow and capacity, traffic/transportation operations, traffic control devices, pedestrian/bicycle facilities, and surface transit operations to traffic safety and advanced analytical methods. The course is taught by a team of professional engineers and planners who practice in the private and public sectors with a collective experience exceeding 100 years. Key learning concepts to be highlighted throughout the three days of intensive training include: managing conflict between/among surface modes, striving for a balanced approach to promoting multiple modes along the same right-of-way (ROW) or crossing each other, promoting safety between modes and for each mode on local streets and roads, options for separating or prioritizing modes in layered networks, planning for multimodal travel at the local level wherever possible, managing multimodal transportation operations efficiently, promoting economic development and livability (in addition to access and mobility), and the best practices in multimodal surface transportation infrastructure planning and sustainable land development for livability. Topics IncludeThe Multimodal Transportation Planning Process and Legal Framework Data Collection, Quantitative Analysis, and Travel Forecasts Environmental Analysis and CEQA New Trends (SB 743) Evaluation and Prioritization of Multimodal Transportation Projects Public Participation & Involvement, Dealing with Controversy Freeway Multimodal Considerations The New Transit/Multimodal Role for Arterials and Collectors Multimodal Traffic Signals Pedestrians and ADA Accommodations: It's the Law Pedestrian Safety and Economic Development Residential Streets: Livability and Quality of Life Multimodal Auditing Techniques and Walking Tour On-Street Bicycling and Ensuring Bicycle Safety Bicycle Paths: Putting it All Together Surface Mass Transit Planning Concepts Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) & Light Rail Transit (LRT) Design Elements and Issues What You Will Learn Attendees will gain an understanding and appreciation of the necessary balance of all surface modes in building, operating and maintaining a functional and multi-modal infrastructure. Multi-modal streets that make effective and efficient use of rights-of-way represent an essential framework for developing and maintaining vital urban and suburban centers and neighborhoods. Trainees will learn the planning role of multimodal surface transportation in the U.S. today, and the processes that are used to achieve planning objectives, including how data is collected and used in multimodal transportation analyses. Attendees will gain an understanding of how regional plans and forecasts affect local land use and transportation plans. They will also learn how environmental analyses and public participation fit within the multimodal transportation planning process, including key impacts on existing networks, legal requirements, and how to resolve conflicts of multimodal transportation projects. In addition, attendees will:Learn the basic principles for highway operations in California, the latest innovations of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) in freeway multimodal functions, and how to relate regional travel pricing policies to successful multimodal operations (e.g., Bay Area) Learn about parallel relationships of multimodal measures on arterial and collector streets for proper freeway operation and multimodal interactions, as they meet over critical junctions such as signalized intersections Learn a full range of treatments for pedestrian and bicycle movement in urban and suburban communities alongside a successful movement of vehicles, including bus priority considerations and success stories throughout the state and nation, with a focus on available tools and design techniques in harmony with the complete streets concepts Learn about the effects of parking considerations as well as innovative pricing programs (e.g., SF Park) and how they influence modal choice and healthy economic development Learn the key design and operational strategies to improve the safety and mobility of bicyclists in a multimodal environment and gain an understanding of which bikeway design options are appropriate for land use contexts in the state Learn how the various transit modes are essential components of well-planned communities from big cities, such as Los Angeles and San Francisco, to suburban municipalities to small towns Learn key planning, design, and operational elements pertaining to LRT and BRT in a multimodal operational environment (e.g., Gold Line LRT, Van Ness BRT) Learn how to better integrate public transit modes with each other, with other modes of surface transportation, and with land use; and the role of the state's metropolitan regions and local governments in this integration Who Should Attend This course is intended for local (i.e., cities and counties) urban planners, transportation planners, and planning technicians, as well as transportation and land use consultants. Both new and experienced planners will benefit from this course. The course is primarily appropriate for urban and suburban perspectives, but may be relevant to rural areas that are subject to urban growth challenges.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar (Postdoc)
events.description: Cris Woroch, Arnold O. Beckman Postdoctoral Fellow, UC BerkeleyPolymer design with new monomers & post-polymerization modificationsPolymeric materials are essential for modern life, but current production and disposal methods pose significant environmental harm. Most commodity polymers are constructed from a small set of petrochemical precursors that are non-renewable, are carbon-intensive to produce, yield materials that are challenging to recycle, and offer limited chemical diversity. My work focuses on designing new materials from renewable feedstocks and new methods to upcycle the materials used today. I will present recent work on the construction of new materials from lignocellulose-based furfural and carbon dioxide and the selective oxidation of polyethylene surfaces. In each, I will highlight how careful control of polymer microstructure yields new properties not met by commodity materials.Biography: Cristián (Cris) Woroch is originally from Oakland, California. He earned his undergraduate degree in chemistry at Pomona College, where he worked as a Beckman Scholar with Prof. Nicholas Ball to develop SuFEx methods for medicinal chemistry. In 2019, he moved to Stanford University for his graduate studies with Prof. Matthew Kanan. In his Ph.D. work, he developed new methods of synthesizing performance-advantaged polymers from lignocellulose and carbon dioxide as an NSF Graduate Research Fellow and Center for Molecular Analysis and Design (CMAD) Fellow. During his graduate studies, he also worked at the National Laboratory of the Rockies in the BOTTLE Consortium under Dr. Gregg Beckham as a DOE Science Graduate Research Fellow and at X, the Moonshot Factory (formerly known as Google X) as a Ph.D. Resident in plastics recycling on Project Materra. Currently, he is an Arnold O. Beckman Postdoctoral Fellow at UC Berkeley with Prof. John Hartwig, where he studies catalytic post-polymerization modification approaches for polymer upcycling.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. events.title: Finding Your Northern Star: Designing Work That Aligns with Who You Are (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) Many professionals reach a point where their role no longer feels fully aligned with who they are, what they value, or how they want to contribute. This sense of being "stuck" can lead to disengagement, uncertainty, or the feeling that one's potential is underutilized — even in meaningful work. This interactive workshop offers participants space to pause, reflect, and reconnect with a clearer sense of direction. Using the concept of a personal Northern Star, participants will explore how their talents, aspirations, and the causes they care about can be integrated into a guiding framework for career decisions. Rather than assuming that fulfillment requires an immediate job change, the session expands the conversation to include multiple pathways for alignment: reshaping aspects of a current role, integrating meaningful work through projects or hobbies, or intentionally preparing for a future transition. Through a guided Northern Star exercise and a priority-mapping activity, participants will identify what matters most to them at this stage of their career, recognize areas of alignment and misalignment, and clarify where they want to invest their time and energy. events.title: North Korea's Messianic Cause
events.organizer: Berkeley Center for the Study of Religion
events.description: What if North Korea was understood less as a nuclear-armed nation state and more as a religious society, one built around worship of the Kim family? It's not as far-fetched as you think. Pyongyang is already the center of one of human history's greatest personality cults: One populated by thousands of statues, busts, mosaics, obelisks, museums and monuments dedicated to state founder Kim Il Sung and his son and grandson, Kim Jong Il and Kim Jong Un. But before Pyongyang was known as the capital of the Kim dynasty, it was better known as the "Jerusalem of the East," the most thoroughly Christianized city in all of Asia. Among the earliest and most fervent converts to the brand of American Presbyterianism that arrived in the city in the late nineteenth century were the very parents and grandparents of Kim Il Sung. Kim grew up in a devout home, attending church every Sunday, teaching Sunday school, performing in church plays and learning to play the organ. The doctrine and ritual he imbibed as a young boy helped him shape the core of the state that he would rule, beginning at age 33 in 1945, until his death a half century later.Jonathan Cheng is the China bureau chief for The Wall Street Journal, overseeing coverage of the world's second-largest economy across politics, economics, business, technology, and society. Jonathan leads a team of two dozen correspondents and researchers in Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Taipei, Singapore, and New York, with responsibility for the Chinese mainland and Taiwan. Previously, Jonathan was the Korea bureau chief for The Journal, running coverage of North Korea and South Korean politics and business. He began his career as an intern in The Journal's Hong Kong bureau and also worked as a markets reporter in The Journal's New York office. Jonathan speaks English, Cantonese and Mandarin Chinese, French, and Korean. A native of Toronto, Jonathan graduated from Princeton University with a degree in history. He lives in Beijing and has traveled to North Korea twice.

events.title: David Chandler Lecture in Physical Chemistry
events.description: Nancy Makri, Professor, University of IllinoisReal-Time Path Integral Methodology for Quantum Dynamics in Condensed-Phase EnvironmentsSince the mid-1990s the iterative, tensor-based quasi-adiabatic propagator path integral (QuAPI) methodology has enabled numerically exact, fully quantum mechanical simulations of system-bath dynamics. Recent work showed that one can further disentangle the path integral variables through the rigorous small matrix decomposition (SMatPI), which leads to iterative propagation with matrices of minimal size equal to that of the system's reduced density matrix (RDM). By eliminating tensor storage, the SMatPI algorithm enables the simulation of multistate systems and long-memory processes. Combination with modular path integral (MPI) decompositions suitable to systems with a locally one-dimensional topology enables iteration in space and time, leading to linear scaling with system size and propagation length. The methodology has been extended to anharmonic environments, whose effects on the RDM can be equivalent to those from an effective harmonic bath or give rise to novel features arising from essential, non-removable anharmonicity. Recent work has shown that the quantum paths entering the path integral expression can be mapped on graphs, whose properties can be exploited to arrive at novel algorithms that allow the efficient treatment of static disorder and the simulation of processes that involve thousands of system states (regardless of the nature of the system Hamiltonian).

events.title: A Journalist's Path to Leadership on Global Justice and Climate
events.description: Nicholas Kristof grew up on an Oregon farm and became a Pulitzer Prize winning columnist for the New York Times, best-selling author and maker of TV documentaries. He has chronicled war, genocide and climate injustice, and has been held at gunpoint in more countries than he cares to remember. Kristof recovers from his travels by raising apples and grapes on his family farm and confronting climate change directly. Nicholas Kristof is a columnist at The New York Times and a two-time winner of the Pulitzer Prize. He grew up on a farm in Oregon, graduated from Harvard, earned a First in law at Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar, and then studied Arabic in Cairo. He was a foreign correspondent for The New York Times in Hong Kong, Beijing and Tokyo, and then served as editor of The Sunday New York Times. After 9/11, he became an op-ed columnist. Aside from his Pulitzers, for coverage of China's Tiananmen democracy movement and for the Darfur genocide, he has won an Emmy and several global humanitarian prizes. He has written six best-selling books, including the No. 1 best-seller Half the Sky and the memoir Chasing Hope, and has made several television documentaries. Kristof, who has lived on four continents and traveled to more than 160 countries, leads an annual fundraising appeal for selected nonprofits that now raises more than $50 million a year.If you have questions about accessibility or require accommodations to participate an event, please contact us at kdarling@berkeley.edu (mailto:kdarling@berkeley.edu) or call (510) 672-1869.

events.title: Catie Cuan // Physical AI: Giving AI a Robot Body
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Dr. Catie Cuan, entrepreneur, engineer, artist, and pioneer in the emerging field of choreorobotics. Working at the intersection of artificial intelligence, robotics, and human-robot interaction, Catie explores how movement shapes the way we perceive and relate to machines. She is the founder of ART Lab (AI Robot Technology), and has led work across institutions including Stanford University and the Exploratorium, where she served as artist in residence. ​In her talk, Physical AI: Giving AI a Robot Body, Catie will explore what happens as AI moves beyond screens and into the physical world. As robots become more intelligent, how they move becomes just as important as what they can do. Drawing on her unique background in dance and robotics, she argues that movement is not just functional, but expressive, shaping emotion, trust, and human connection. Through examples from her work, including training robots to improvise, respond to human gestures, and move collectively, she will show how choreography can inform the design of more intuitive, responsive, and human-centered machines. ​Come experience a glimpse of a future where robots do not just act intelligently, but move with intention, awareness, and a sense of presence that changes how we live alongside them. ​This event is free and open to the public. ……………….. ​Design Field Notes (https://jacobsinstitute.berkeley.edu/design-field-notes/?utm_source=luma) is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.If you require accommodation for a disability for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Jacobs Institute staff atjacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu (mailto:jacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu)with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell.
