events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with David Henkin
events.description: In Out of the Ballpark (Oxford, 2026), David Henkin (History) reconsiders the character, meaning, and delights of baseball by exploring the game's unusual features and the sport's many resonances with other aspects of modern life. To this end, he abandons several assumptions and mythologies that underlie most approaches to histories of baseball: that it is unique among sports and fundamentally different from other kinds of entertainment; that it is specific to the United States; that it has changed fundamentally in recent years; and that the keys to understanding it lie primarily in examining what happens on the field of play. Instead, Henkin moves across time and space to examine baseball's history since the nineteenth century and beyond US borders. He takes readers inside the structures of clubs and leagues, interprets the sacred scripture of rulebooks, and illuminates some of baseball's rites and rituals that are often associated with honor and manhood. He charts baseball's significance along the routes of American and Japanese imperial expansion and the shifting maps of race and ethnicity in the US. Baseball is found at negotiating tables that pit capital against labor and in pivotal moments in the history of mass media. He shows us how baseball might offer a complex and capacious space for thinking about such things as spectatorship, success, community, order, and contingency in the modern world. Henkin is joined by Alva Noë (Philosophy). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Bioengineering Seminar: Activity-Based Assays for Monitoring Treatment and Prevention of Infectious Diseases
events.description: Abstract: For many infectious and chronic diseases, effective medications already exist, and prevention or treatment succeeds or fails on whether those drugs are dosed and taken correctly. Concentrations that are too low lead to new infection or treatment failure, and concentrations that are too high cause adverse reactions. Current methods for measuring drug concentrations are expensive, labor-intensive, and slow, which puts them out of reach for most people who would benefit from them. Rapid and inexpensive tests would make monitoring and dose individualization far more widely available, from centralized laboratories to the bedside and the home, and particularly in resource-limited settings. Our lab develops tests that measure drug concentrations using the drugs' own biochemical activity rather than by detecting the drug molecules themselves. We have built user-friendly tests that measure the active intracellular forms of several human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) medications, with excellent concordance with gold-standard mass spectrometry. We extended this approach to therapeutic drug monitoring of cytomegalovirus (CMV) medications, measuring ganciclovir triphosphate in infants with congenital CMV, where dosing must avoid both underexposure and toxicity. The same need applies to transplant recipients and other immunocompromised populations. Most recently, we inverted our assay principle: by measuring the activity of reverse transcriptase derived from patient samples, rather than recombinant enzyme, we can measure HIV viral load and detect phenotypic drug resistance in the same rapid and user-friendly format. Our current focus is on optimizing, validating, and delivering these tests to populations in need both locally and globally, building a unified toolkit for monitoring drug exposure, viral suppression, and drug resistance at the point of need.

events.title: Camilla Maiani | Marie Curie (1867-1934): The Making of a Myth
events.description: Marie Curie is one of the most famous scientists in modern history. She is especially celebrated for her pioneering work on radioactivity, and for being the only person to have received two Nobel prizes, in Physics and in Chemistry. Over time, she has also become an iconic figure for feminists and women in science. But behind the myth lies a much more complex figure, firmly rooted in the social and cultural context of her time. This conference explores Marie Curie's scientific achievements, while examining how her public image was shaped during her lifetime - particularly during her first official visit to the United States - and how it continued to change after her death in 1934. Camilla Maiani has a PhD and a background in particle physics research and has worked at the CEA and the Université d'Orsay in collaboration with the CERN laboratories in Geneva. Today, she is a science and science history outreach specialist at the Curie Museum in Paris, where she develops educational content based on the museum's collections. events.title: Jeffrey Bowers: Research in NeuroAI should focus more on the findings and methods of psychology to advance our understanding of biological intelligence
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - All that is compute transforms into concrete: Monopoly rent and the fixity of AI's infrastructure
events.description: In the capitalist imaginary, artificial intelligence is narrated on dematerialization. In this telling, capital has escaped the weight of human labor via the frictionless circulation of data. This paper argues the opposite: the AI economy is a geography of fixity, where training large language models requires warehouse-scale data centers anchored to specific territories by the demands of energy, infrastructure, and available land. Two analytical categories theorize this fixity. The first concerns the monopoly control of location and network proximity: value is extracted from whoever sits closest to the data, controls the interconnection, and commands the lowest latency. The second concerns the monopoly control of computation itself: training frontier AI models is capital-intensive, technically scarce, and concentrated in a handful of firms who can extract a tribute that is not reducible to productivity but to infra/structural position. Both forms of extraction are rent. And both are responses to a profitability crisis in the AI sector driven by rising fixed capital requirements that outpace returns. We draw on financial filings, industry reports, and field observations in Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley to show that what appears as an agglomeration economy is better understood as rent extracted through the strategic fixity of capital in digital infrastructure. Dillon Mahmoudi (dillonm@umbc.edu) is an Associate Professor of Geography and Environmental Systems at the University of Maryland Baltimore County. and Alan Wiig (alanwiig@ufl.edu) is an Associate Professor of Geography at the University of Florida. They recently published a book chapter, Land for AI: Data Center Real Estate Markets in The Inner World of Artificial Intelligence (2026).

events.title: Matrix on Point: The State of U.S. Immigration Enforcement and Surveillance
events.description: REGISTER Federal immigration enforcement in the United States is increasingly shaped by the convergence of surveillance technologies, data systems, and on-the-ground policing practices. From AI-assisted identification tools to information-sharing across agencies, these developments are transforming how enforcement operates, and raising urgent questions about civil liberties and democratic oversight. This panel will bring together scholars to examine the social and political consequences, and the stakes for rights in an era of technological governance. The panel will feature David Hausman, Assistant Professor at UC Berkeley Law School, Caitlin Patler, Associate Professor of Public Policy at the UC Berkeley Goldman School of Public Policy, and Jennifer Urban, Clinical Professor of Law at UC Berkeley Law School. Deirdre Mulligan, Professor in the UC Berkeley School of Information, will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the Asian American Research Center, the Center for Race and Gender, the Berkeley Interdisciplinary Migration Initiative, the Goldman School of Public Policy, and the UC Berkeley School of Information.Matrix On Point (https://matrix.berkeley.edu/category/event-type/matrix-on-point/) is a discussion series promoting focused, cross-disciplinary conversations on today's most pressing issues. Offering opportunities for scholarly exchange and interaction, each Matrix On Point features the perspectives of leading scholars and specialists from different disciplines, followed by an open conversation. These thought-provoking events are free and open to the public. Panelists David Hausman (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/our-faculty/faculty-profiles/david-hausman/#tab_profile) is an Assistant Professor at Berkeley Law School. He does empirical work on U.S. immigration enforcement, mostly using government data disclosed in response to Freedom of Information Act requests. He also co-directs the Deportation Data Project (https://deportationdata.org/). Before joining Berkeley, he practiced law at the ACLU Immigrants' Rights Project in New York City.Caitlin Patler (https://gspp.berkeley.edu/research-and-impact/faculty/caitlin-patler) is Associate Professor of Public Policy at the UC Berkeley Goldman School of Public Policy, and faculty affiliate of the Berkeley Interdisciplinary Migration Initiative (BIMI), Berkeley Population Center, and the Institute for Research on Labor and Employment. Dr. Patler's research examines US immigration and criminal laws, legal statuses, and law enforcement institutions as drivers of socioeconomic and health disparities.Jennifer M. Urban (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/our-faculty/faculty-profiles/jennifer-urban/#tab_profile) is a Clinical Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law, where she is Director of Policy Initiatives at the Samuelson Law, Technology & Public Policy Clinic (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/experiential/clinics/samuelson-law-technology-public-policy-clinic/). Her research focuses on information policy: intellectual property, privacy and data protection, and security. She regularly collaborates with technologists and academics in disciplines other than law to develop empirically grounded understandings of how new technologies and the regulatory structures around them interact with civil liberties, innovation, and creative expression. In March 2021, Urban was appointed by California Governor Gavin Newsom to be the inaugural Chair of the California Privacy Protection Agency Board.Deirdre K. Mulligan (https://www.ischool.berkeley.edu/people/deirdre-mulligan) (moderator) is a Professor in the School of Information at UC Berkeley, a faculty Director of the Berkeley Center for Law & Technology (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/research/bclt/), and a co-organizer of the Algorithmic Fairness & Opacity Working Group (http://afog.berkeley.edu/). Mulligan's research explores legal and technical means of protecting values such as privacy, freedom of expression, and fairness in socio-technical systems. Her book Privacy on the Ground: Driving Corporate Behavior in the United States and Europe (https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/privacy-ground), a study of privacy practices in large corporations in five countries, with UC Berkeley Law Prof. Kenneth Bamberger was published in 2015 by MIT Press. Mulligan served as Principal Deputy U.S. Chief Technology Officer at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, (https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp/) and Director of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Office (NAIIO), in the Biden-Harris Administration. In November 2025, Mulligan was appointed to Governor Newsom's California Innovation Council. REGISTER

events.title: EECS Colloquium: Compiler 2.0: Building the Next Generation of Compilers with Machine Learning
events.description: The genius of FORTRAN, introduced in 1957, was not just that it was the first widely successful high-level language, but that it made hardware disappear. The same FORTRAN program could run on an IBM System/360, a DEC PDP-8, a CDC 6600, or even a Cray-1, with enough performance that most programmers never had to touch assembly or write architecture-specific code. Over time, as both hardware and software grew more complex, compilers quietly lost much of their ability to maintain this abstraction. Multicores, complex vector instructions, and specialized accelerators have pushed more of the performance burden back onto the programmer. Today, we have, in many ways, come full circle. For example, getting peak performance from NVIDIA's V100, A100, H100, and B100 generations often requires different, architecture-specific CUDA kernels and, on the latest parts, even hand-written PTX assembly to fully exploit tensor cores and the Tensor Memory Accelerator. To the best of our knowledge, the Apple/Arm SME accelerator does not even have a high-level compiler, and most high-performance code must be written using intrinsics or assembly. The recent AI revolution is bringing capabilities that are poised to upend the traditional compiler. Machine learning can give existing compilers capabilities they have never had, from making complex optimization decisions to generating substantial portions of compiler passes. At the extreme, LLMs may replace much of the traditional compiler as we know it. This raises a fundamental question: can the next generation of compilers finally fulfill the promise that began with FORTRAN? Can they transform a single, high-level description of an algorithm into light-speed implementations across CPUs, GPUs, and specialized accelerators, while once again making the underlying hardware disappear? In this talk, I will hallucinate about this exciting possibility, drawing lessons from the history of compiler research and exploring possible paths toward building Compiler 2.0. Saman Amarasinghe is the Thomas and Gerd Perkins Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), where he leads the Commit Compiler Research Group. Under his leadership, the Commit group has developed a wide range of innovative programming languages and compilers, including StreamIt, StreamJIT, PetaBricks, Halide, TACO, Finch, SySTeC, GraphIt, Simit, MILK, Cimple, BioStream, NetBlocks, BREeze, CoLa, Shim, AskIt, and Seq. Additionally, the group has created compiler and runtime frameworks such as DynamoRIO, Helium, Tiramisu, Codon, BuildIt, and D2X, as well as vectorization techniques and tools such as Superword Level Parallelism (SLP), goSLP, and VeGen. Saman's team also developed Ithemal, a machine-learning-based performance predictor; Program Shepherding, which protects programs from external attacks; the extensible OpenTuner autotuning framework; and Kendo, a deterministic execution system. He co-led the Raw architecture project. Outside academia, Saman has founded or co-founded several companies, including Determina, Lanka Internet Services Ltd., Venti Technologies, DataCebo, Exaloop, and Build4Sim. He earned his BS in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from Cornell University in 1988, and his MSEE and Ph.D. from Stanford University in 1990 and 1997, respectively. He is a Fellow of the ACM and a recipient of the ACM-IEEE CS Ken Kennedy Award.

events.title: MBN Seminar: Leveraging Big Data from Human Cohorts to Reveal the Biology of Thermogenic Fat
events.description: Paul Cohen, M.D., Ph.D., Albert Resnick,M.D. Associate Professor, Head, Weslie R. and William H. Janeway Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism, The Rockefeller UniversityTitle: Leveraging Big Data from Human Cohorts to Reveal the Biology of Thermogenic FatSummary: Over 2 billion adults worldwide are overweight or obese, and excess body weight significantly increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, cardiovascular disease, and many types of cancer. Little is known about how obesity contributes to the pathogenesis of these diseases, which in aggregate are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in much of the world. My laboratory focuses on understanding how obesity leads to metabolic diseases and cancer with the ultimate goal of developing therapies to break the link between them. Obesity is defined by excess white fat, which contributes to associated diseases, but mammals also possess brown fat, which can convert chemical energy into heat. We have contributed to a fundamental understanding of molecular and tissue-level regulation of brown fat, but this tissue was long thought to have a limited role in human physiology. We have used a large patient cohort study to show that brown fat is in fact associated with significant metabolic and cardiovascular health benefits. My research program investigates the biology and genetics of brown fat to understand how it mediates these pleiotropic effects. Centered on human biology and employing unique patient cohorts and novel imaging and biochemical methods, we take a systems-based approach to dissect the role of brown fat in health and disease.

events.title: Neyman Statistics Seminar with Yizhe Zhu: Differentially private synthetic data generation
events.description: Abstract: Differentially private synthetic data enables the sharing and analysis of sensitive datasets while providing rigorous privacy guarantees for individual contributors. A central challenge is to preserve the information needed for meaningful downstream analysis. Many existing methods aim to preserve a broad range of statistical properties, but their accuracy can deteriorate as the number of variables grows. This motivates approaches that exploit structure in the data and in the statistical questions of interest. In this talk, I will present a sequence of works on efficient private synthetic data generation and explain how low-dimensional data structure and smoothness in the statistical quantities of interest can yield improved accuracy with nearly optimal guarantees. I will also introduce a general moment-matching framework for constructing private synthetic data tailored to the chosen class of queries. Bio: Yizhe Zhu is an Assistant Professor of Mathematics at the University of Southern California. His research lies at the intersection of probability and mathematical data science, with an emphasis on random matrices and tensors, high-dimensional inference, and differential privacy. Before joining USC, he was a Visiting Assistant Professor at the University of California, Irvine, and a postdoctoral fellow at the Simons Laufer Mathematical Sciences Institute in Berkeley. He earned his Ph.D. in Mathematics from the University of California, San Diego, in 2021.

events.title: Laura Sánchez Carrasco & Íñigo Cobeta: What Space Builds | Architecture Lecture Series
events.description: Laura Sánchez Carrasco is an architect and associate professor at the Escuela Técnica Superior de Arquitectura, UPM, where she has taught since 2018. She holds a degree in architecture (2007), a master's in analysis, theory, and history of architecture (2014), and a PhD cum laude (2017), all from UPM. Her research addresses postwar North American architecture and its connections with Spanish architecture, combining architectural history with digital methods of historiographic analysis. She is currently part of the research project "Conexiones de la arquitectura española con las Américas (1976–2006)" and has previously collaborated with MIT on the project "Mapping Global Architectural Histories on Modernism". Alongside her academic career, she practiced architecture professionally for nearly 20 years, both running her own studio and working within established firms, where she led competition-winning projects from design through construction. Íñigo Cobeta is a researcher and associate professor in the Department of Architectural Composition at the Escuela Técnica Superior de Arquitectura de Madrid (ETSAM), where he has taught since 2006. He has collaborated with specialized international publications such as ArquitecturaCOAM or RITA. He has also acted as an independent national curator (Bienal Iberoamericana de Arquitectura y Urbanismo 2006). For 20 years he worked as an architect, collaborating with MoneoBrockStudio on the Termas de Tiberio in the Panticosa Spa and developing his own practice. In 2019, the bicentennial of the Museo Nacional del Prado, he was invited to lecture on some of the conclusions of his thesis, The Prado, from Territory to Stage, directed by Rafael Moneo. He is currently part of the research project "Conexiones de la arquitectura española con las Américas (1976–2006)". Since 2020, he has focused on teaching, research, and developing experimental projects on public schools.

events.description: The VIDRINE presents four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels. — Presented in partnership by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative, Worth Ryder Gallery, and the The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here Curatorial and Artist team.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. events.title: Marius Wernig: Human iPS cell-derived microtissues to study neurodegenerative disease
events.description: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and embryonic stem cells (ESCs) have become valuable tools to investigate disease mechanisms because they can be differentiated into various somatic cell types, including those of the central nervous system (CNS), which are difficult to obtain from primary sources. Microglia are the immune cells of the central nervous system and are thought to be key players in both physiological and disease conditions. Several microglial features are poorly conserved between mice and human, such as the function of the neurodegeneration-associated immune receptor Trem2. iPSC-derived microglia offer a powerful opportunity to generate and study human microglia. However, human iPSC-derived microglia often exhibit activated phenotypes in vitro, and assessing their impact on other brain cell types remains challenging due to limitations in current co-culture systems. We developed fully defined brain microtissues, composed of human iPSC-derived neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, co-cultured in 2D or 3D formats. Our microtissues are stable and self-sufficient over time, requiring no exogenous cytokines or growth factors. All three cell types exhibit morphologies characteristic of their in vivo environment and show functional properties. Co-cultured microglia develop more homeostatic phenotypes compared to microglia exposed to exogenous cytokines. Hence, these tri-cultures provide a unique approach to investigate cell-cell interactions between brain cell types. We found that astrocytes and not neurons are sufficient for microglial survival and maturation, and that astrocyte-derived M-CSF is essential for microglial survival. Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing analyses nominated a network of reciprocal communication between cell types. Brain microtissues faithfully recapitulated pathogenic α-synuclein seeding and aggregation, suggesting their usefulness as human cell models to study not only normal but also pathological cell biological processes.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: Book Talk: Global Racism – A Challenge for the World
events.organizer: Thelton E. Henderson Center for Social Justice
events.description: Join the Miller Institute for Global Challenges and the Law and the Thelton E. Henderson Center for Social Justice in welcoming Professor Anna Spain Bradley (Distinguished MacArthur Foundation Chair in International Justice and Human Rights, Professor of Law at UCLA School of Law) to UC Berkeley Law. In this lunchtime conversation, Prof. Spain Bradley will discuss her forthcoming book Global Racism: A Challenge for the World. Executive Director Savala Nolan will moderate. All in attendance will be entered in a raffle to receive a free signed copy of the book. For more information about Prof. Spain Bradley and her work, go to her website here: https://annaspainbradley.com/ This event is open to all. Lunch will be served inside of Room 170 starting at 12:50 PM. RSVPs will be prioritized. RSVP Here From Website: Anna Spain Bradley is an author, award-winning legal scholar, higher education leader, and globally recognized human rights expert. She holds the MacArthur Foundation Chair in International Justice and Human Rights and is a Professor of Law at UCLA School of Law. With two decades of experience studying the role of law in promoting peace, dignity, and human rights around the world, she has devoted over ten years to leadership roles in higher education, including as UCLA’s Vice Chancellor for Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion. Her latest book, Global Racism: A Challenge for the World, (Oxford University Press, October 2026), articulates the phenomenon of global racism as a universally available form of oppression operating on a global scale that interacts with the human ecosystem and world order. Global racism poses a serious threat to humanity, capable of existing anywhere and everywhere. Professor Spain Bradley takes readers on a journey across continents and centuries, reimagining the fight against racism as a fight for our shared humanity. Jared Diamond, Pulitzer Prize-winning author of Guns, Germs, and Steel, writes, “This powerful, compelling book exposes racism as a global phenomenon. It thrives in countries from Albania to the USA. It targets peoples from Asians and Africans to Jews, Roma, and Ukrainians. You’ll come to realize: in today’s globalized world, racism imperils not only its victims, but also its perpetrators.” Global Racism builds upon Professor Spain Bradley’s pioneering legal scholarship “Human Rights Racism” (Harvard Human Rights Journal, 2019) identifying racism as an undefined violation of human rights under international law. Her first book Human Choice in International Law (Cambridge University Press, 2021) challenges traditional assumptions about rationality in legal decision making by introducing insights from neuroscience to the study of international legal and political decision making.

events.title: Performing Enlightenment: Buddhism and Theater in Early Modern China | Lecture by Mengxiao Wang
events.description: In late Ming and early Qing China, a major revival of Buddhism coincided with a growing fascination with theater. In Performing Enlightenment, Mengxiao Wang examines how Chinese Buddhist monastics and laypeople actively engaged with and transformed the dramatic arts. Drawing on a wide range of religious and literary sources, the book argues that Buddhist practitioners reconciled the tension between spiritual cultivation and worldly entertainment by reimagining theater as a creative mode of devotion. In this process, playwriting, stage performance, and theatergoing all emerged as legitimate pathways to enlightenment. Speaker Bio:Mengxiao Wang is Assistant Professor of Chinese Literature in the Department of East Asian Languages and Cultures at the University of Southern California. She received her Ph.D. from Yale University and was the Sheng Yen Postdoctoral Fellow in Chinese Buddhism at UC Berkeley. Her research explores the intersections of literature and Buddhism in early modern China, with particular attention to theater, ritual, gender, and book history. Her first monograph, Performing Enlightenment: Buddhism and Theater in Early Modern China, was published by the Harvard University Asia Center in 2026. This event is co-sponsored by the Numata Center for Buddhist Studies.

events.title: A Poet in Search of Time: O Changhwan in Moscow
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Janet Poole (University of Toronto) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: Modernist poet O Changhwan left one of the most voluminous literary records of the interregnum—that period marked by the collapse of the Japanese Empire in 1945, dual occupations, and the eruption of civil war in the late 1940s. In such an eventful era, it is perhaps not surprising that survival was on O's mind: survival as a poet, as an aspiring socialist, as a living being. My talk begins and ends with O's poetic travelogue of his 1949 journey to Moscow for medical treatment, but I understand that journey to have begun with his earlier decision to cross the 38th parallel and move to the northern zone of the Korean Peninsula in 1947. In reading O's poems, translations and essays from the interregnum, I hope to write a more provisional history of an early Cold War modernism, one shaped by decolonization and the refusal of anticommunism, and one that sought a home, however transiently, in the nascent revolutionary-socialist state of North Korea. Speaker Bio: Janet Poole teaches in the fields of Korean literature and literary translation at the University of Toronto. Her most recent book Patterns of the Heart and Other Stories (Columbia University Press, 2024) presents an introduction to the little known modernist writer Ch'oe Myŏngik (1903-?). Born and based in Pyongyang throughout his career, Ch'oe's work lovingly details life in that city and chronicles the hopes and dreams for a new society in the age of decolonization. A dedicated literary translator, Poole has also translated works by mid-twentieth century writer Yi T'aejun (1904-?), publishing a collection of his anecdotal essays (Eastern Sentiments) and a selection of his short stories (Dust and Other Stories). A new book project, "Decolonizing Style: Going North and the History of Korean Modernism," looks at the writings of Korea's modernist writers and artists who crossed the 38th parallel into what was to become the Democratic People's Republic in the late 1940s. The project follows upon an earlier study of modernist responses to the fascist regime of the late colonial era, When the Future Disappears: The Modernist Imagination in Late Colonial Korea (Columbia University Press, 2014).

events.title: Naeem Mohaiemen | Celluloid Frontiers: A Missing Can of Film and Stop Genocide
events.description: In conjunction with the exhibition Private Frontiers (https://bampfa.org/program/campus-collaborations-private-frontiers-media-legacies-cold-war), BAMPFA presents A Missing Can of Film (2025), a 44-minute essay film by artist and filmmaker Naeem Mohaiemen. Commissioned by the EVA International and the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, the project explores the legacy of slain Bangladeshi filmmaker Zahir Raihan and the unresolved complexities of the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War The screening will include a conversation between Naeem Mohaiemen (https://www.shobak.org/there) and Tausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor), Assistant Curator at BAMPFA. Co-sponsored by the Institute for South Asia Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (http://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/), and the South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/initiatives/SAAI) at UC Berkeley. —DATE: Thu, Oct 29, 2026 TIME: 7-8 pm PST VENUE: BAMPFA TICKETS: Tickets for BAMPFA members are now on sale.Tickets for the general public go on sale Friday, August 7 at 11 AM. Buy tickets HERE (https://secure.bampfa.org/33280/33347?_gl=1*ev5un9*_ga*NzQxNDczMzYzLjE3ODU5NjA0MTU.*_ga_SDH80YD3Z1*czE3ODU5NjA0MTUkbzEkZzEkdDE3ODU5NjA5OTAkajYwJGwwJGgw) —About the Film Commissioned by EVA Ireland International and the Kochi-Muziris Biennale, AMissing Can of Film (2025) traces the lost-left politics buried within Zahir Raihan's Stop Genocide (1971)—a film edited in the style of Soviet Realism and Third Cinema during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War. Raihan, a novelist and director, was abducted only forty-five days after the end of the war. A Missing Can of Film combines scenes from Stop Genocide with footage shot at the Bangladesh Film Development Corporation after the nation's 2024 July Student "Monsoon" Uprising, interrogating the film canister as a vessel of contested history.About the Artist/FilmmakerNaeem Mohaiemen (https://www.shobak.org/there) imagines rhizomatic families, malleable borders, and socialist utopias– beginning from postcolonial markers and then radiating outward to unlikely transnational alliances. In spite of underscoring a tendency toward misrecognition of allies, the hope of a future global left, against current categories of race, religion and nation, drives the work. He is author of Prisoners of Shothik Itihash (Kunsthalle Basel, 2014); editor of Chittagong Hill Tracts in the Blind Spot of Bangladesh Nationalism (Drishtipat, 2010); and co-editor w/ Lorenzo Fusi of System Error: War is a Force that Gives us Meaning (Sylvana, 2007).About the DiscussantTausif Noor (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/tausif-noor) is Assistant Curator at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, where he helped organize the exhibition To Exalt the Ephemeral: The (Im)Permanent Collection. He previously worked as the Spiegel-Wilks Curatorial Fellow at the Institute of Contemporary Art at the University of Pennsylvania and at the Whitney Museum of American Art. Noor's writing, for which he has received awards from the Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant and the Robert B. Silvers Foundation, has been published in various periodicals and journals, including the New Yorker, the New York Times, the New York Review of Books, Art History, and Artforum, as well as in various artist catalogues and edited volumes. He holds degrees from Dartmouth College and Goldsmiths, University of London and is a PhD candidate in History of Art at the University of California, Berkeley. ————————- Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952).PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking is not always easily available in Berkeley. events.title: America at 250: Reimagining Who We Are
events.description: As the United States marks its 250th anniversary, UC Berkeley invites the campus and the broader community to reflect on a defining question: What vision will guide America’s next 250 years? For two and a half centuries, the United States has been shaped by the aspirations of its founding and by continual debates over identity, belonging, rights, responsibilities, and democratic ideals. Yet many of the institutions that define public life were created for a very different country — demographically, economically, technologically, and culturally. Faculty, scholars, innovators, journalists, and civic leaders come together for a half-day symposium to explore how the United States can renew its democratic promise and foster a stronger sense of belonging and common purpose in an increasingly diverse and interconnected society. Rather than simply commemorating the past, we look ahead: How can we build and sustain a country that truly secures life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness for all—and how can each of us help shape the next chapter of the American experiment? Co-Hosts: UC Berkeley Law, UC Berkeley Journalism, Goldman School of Public Policy, and the Othering & Belonging Institute For accessibility requests, please email elismart@berkeley.edu.

events.title: Bergman Lecture in Inorganic Chemistry
events.description: Karen Goldberg, Vagelos Professor of Energy Research, University of PennsylvaniaOrganometallic Complexes and Molecular Oxygen: Developing Mechanistic UnderstandingMolecular oxygen represents the ideal oxidant to use in chemical oxidations. It is abundantly available, inexpensive (particularly if used without separation from air) and environmentally benign. However, in homogeneous metal-catalyzed organic oxidations, more expensive and/or hazardous oxidants are often employed. A limiting factor in the development of homogeneous catalytic systems for aerobic oxidations has been a lack of mechanistic understanding of exactly how transition metal complexes react with molecular oxygen. Traditionally, organometallic chemists rigorously protect their compounds from oxygen and so our knowledge of the reactivity of organometallic compounds and oxygen is severely underdeveloped. In this presentation, kinetic and mechanistic studies of the reactions of molecular oxygen with several late metal complexes will be presented along with our nascent understanding of the various mechanistic pathways available for oxygen insertion reactions. The opportunities and potential for the incorporation of such reactions into hydrocarbon functionalization strategies will also be discussed.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Fermionic optimal transport
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Paola Zurlo, Universita degli Studi Aldo Moro, Bari, ItalyWe consider optimal transport between quantum dynamical systems on $Z_2$ graded von Neumann algebras. In the usual, non-graded setting , Wassersrein distances between quantum systems can be defined in terms of transport plans of tensor products involving the commutant of one of the algebras. We briefly recall this construction and describe its extension to the graded setting, where the usual commutant and tensor product are replaced by the twisted commutant and the Fermi tensor product. The main point of the construction is a correspondence between fermionic and usual transport plans. More precisely, using cyclic representations associated with transport plans and the Klein isomorphisms induced by the gradings, we establish a one-to-one correspondencebetween fermionic transport plans and graded transport plans in the usual tensor product. This correspondence allows the Wasserstein distances in the fermionic setting to be related to the corresponding distances in the non-graded setting, and in particular yields their metric properties.

events.title: The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing
events.description: The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing Monday, November 2, 12:30 - 2:00 pm *Lunchtime talk* Institute of International Studies 223 Philosophy HallREGISTER (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/1Rd-bqIFW9uq2WJK95uHg8WOYJHOAI14DXYfJCj-d0fk/edit) The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing (Cambridge University Press, 2026) examines the politics of Tunisia after the Arab Spring. Tunisia emerged as the one success story to transition to democracy, winning a Nobel Peace Prize in 2015 for its focus on inclusion and power-sharing. How, then, did its democracy collapse in 2021? Drawing on unique interviews with senior Tunisian officials, alongside three nationally representative surveys of the population, The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy points to an overemphasis on compromise, consensus, and power-sharing. Although power-sharing institutions can be useful at the start of a transition, the book finds that extending them beyond that point can lead democracy to unravel by frustrating voters and spurring the rise of populists and extremists. The book takes an in-depth look at Tunisia's transition and then explores how far the theory travels through a quantitative analysis of all democratic transitions between 1942–2020. Overall, the book reveals the dark side of power-sharing, broadening our understanding of the causes of populism, polarization, and democratic breakdown. Sharan Grewal is an Associate Professor of Government at American University (https://www.american.edu/spa/faculty/sgrewal.cfm) and a Nonresident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution (https://www.brookings.edu/experts/sharan-grewal/). He was previously assistant professor at William & Mary and a research fellow at the Middle East Initiative (https://www.belfercenter.org/person/sharan-grewal) at Harvard. He received a PhD in Politics from Princeton University in 2018. Sharan's research examines revolutions and democratic transitions, particularly in the Arab world. His first book, Soldiers of Democracy? Military Legacies and the Arab Spring (Oxford University Press, 2023), explores the conditions under which militaries support or thwart democratic transitions, drawing on interviews and surveys of military personnel in Egypt and Tunisia. It received APSA's Best Book in MENA Politics (https://apsamena.org/2024/10/19/2023-mena-politics-section-award-winners/) Award and the Robert Jervis Best International Security Book (https://apsanet.org/membership/organized-sections/organized-section-awards/past-awards/section-19/) Award. His second book, The Rise and Fall of Tunisian Democracy: Populism, Polarization, and the Perils of Power-Sharing, is forthcoming with Cambridge University Press in October 2026. Sharan's work has also been published in the American Political Science Review, American Journal of Political Science, and British Journal of Political Science, among other journals. These papers have explored when Islamists become democrats, how discrimination shapes Muslim migrants, and why US training politicizes foreign militaries. These pieces have won Best Paper and Article Awards from APSA MENA and APSA's Democracy & Autocracy section, as well as the Perry World House-Foreign Affairs Emerging Scholars Prize. Sharan's research has received funding from the National Science Foundation, the Henry Luce Foundation, the John Templeton Foundation, the Smith Richardson Foundation, and the Defense Security Cooperation University. He writes regularly about Middle East politics for Brookings andthe Washington Post, and has been interviewed by the New York Times, Wall Street Journal, and Reuters, among others. He serves on the editorial board of the journal Comparative Politics.

events.title: Shu-ou Shan: "Accurate Decision Making during Protein Biogenesis"
events.description: Proper protein biogenesis is a pre-requisite for the generation and maintenance of a functional proteome. Accumulating data show that this process begins early, when nascent proteins emerge from the ribosome. Within seconds, the nascent polypeptide must engage the correct set of biogenesis factors and commit to the proper biogenesis pathway. These early decisions profoundly influence the folding, assembly, localization, maturation, and quality control of nascent proteins. How are nascent proteins selected and triaged into the appropriate biogenesis pathways? How does the cellular chaperone network handle aggregation-prone membrane/organellar proteins during their biogenesis? Our work aims to address these fundamental questions at biochemical and biophysical resolution, by integrating quantitative approaches in biochemistry, biophysics and mechanistic enzymology with structural and molecular cell biology. In this talk, I will describe recent work that begin to elucidate how diverse protein biogenesis machinery coordinate in space and time at the ribosome to ensure the efficiency and fidelity of cotranslational protein biogenesis, and how the biophysical properties of nascent proteins shaped the emergence of multi-layered biogenesis pathways.

events.title: Merck Symposium
events.description: Jim Morken, Professor & Louise and Jim Vanderslice and Family Chair, Boston CollegeCatalytic Stereoselective Synthesis with Boron ReagentsChiral organoboronic esters are versatile intermediates for chemical synthesis. Not only are these compounds stable under a variety of reaction conditions, they are generally non-toxic and can be transformed with minimal generation of hazardous waste. An important feature of aliphatic organoboronic esters is that the boron atom may be replaced with an array of different functional groups through efficient, stereospecific transformations. This seminar will cover new strategies for the construction of alkylboronic esters from simple starting materials in a catalytic enantioselective fashion, and will also discuss ways in which these compounds can functionalized by catalytic stereospecific couplings. In addition, application of organoboronate-based transformations to address compelling problems in chemical synthesis will be discussed. Professor James Morken was born in Concord, California and obtained his B.S. in chemistry in 1989 from UC Santa Barbara working with Prof. Bruce Rickborn. He obtained his Ph.D. from Boston College in 1995 with Prof. Amir Hoveyda and was an NSF Postdoctoral Fellow with Stuart Schreiber at Harvard University. In 1997, he became an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He was promoted to Associate Professor in 2002 and in 2006 joined the faculty of Boston College. In 2014, he was named the Louise and James Vanderslice and Family Chaired Professor of Chemistry at Boston College. Professor Morken's research focuses on the development of transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric processes and their use in complex molecule synthesis. He is particularly interested in the study and development of catalytic enantioselective reactions involving organoboron reagents. Because of the broad array of reactions that available to organoboronates, these types of process can be employed to address a number of compelling problems in the construction of organic frameworks.

events.title: Harold S. Johnston Lecture
events.description: Steven Brown, Deputy Director, NOAA Chemical Sciences LaboratoryPyrogenic Skies: Photochemistry, heterogeneous chemistry and air quality impacts of wildfire smoke As wildfires have increased in frequency and intensity across North America, their emissions have become a driver of regional air quality degradation. Biomass burning is a large source of ozone precursors, nitrogen oxides (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), as well as particulate matter that impacts air quality directly and also drives heterogeneous chemical processes. Photochemistry within smoke plumes creates pyrogenic ozone over a variety of timescales, leading to short- and long-range transport and widespread increases in the ozone background. Mixing and entrainment of smoke that is rich in pyrogenic VOCs into NOx-rich urban areas alters regional photochemistry and can further enhance ozone production. However, aerosol loads associated with smoke layers may also suppress photochemistry. Heterogeneous chemistry in smoke plumes influences atmospheric composition through a different set of chemical cycles that affect both the lower and upper atmosphere. A series of recent airborne and ground-based field studies has investigated these chemical processes in biomass burning influenced air. These include the 2019 Fire Influence on Regional to Global Environments and Air Quality (FIREX-AQ), the 2022 California Fire Dynamics Experiment (CalFiDE), the 2023 Atmospheric Emissions and Reactivity Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas (AEROMMA) campaign, the 2024 Utah Summer Ozone study, and others. These studies provide new insights into the biomass burning influence on tropospheric ozone at all scales, from near field plume chemistry to the global remote troposphere, and from the continental background to local urban influence.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Atreyee Gupta
events.description: Atreyee Gupta takes a revelatory look at modernism in India, exploring art's role in decolonization and aesthetic discourse across the Global South. Modernism's peak in the interwar and postwar decades coincided with the eruption of antifascist and decolonization movements globally, including the League against Imperialism, the Bandung Asian-African Conference, and the Non-Aligned Movement. Viewing artistic practices through the lens of the radical intellectual possibilities that these epoch-making events prompted, Atreyee Gupta (History of Art) uncovers a modernist internationalism incongruous with Westernist cultural hegemonies. Modernism, she shows, cannot be separated from concepts of freedom and autonomy generated by Third World political struggles. Gupta mobilizes concepts including liberation, anti-imperialism, development, and modernization as essential analytic categories for art history, reorienting our understanding of both global modernism and Indian art. Intertwining stories of art and liberation, aesthetics and decolonization, and intellectual practices and political revolution in the Third World, or what is now known as the Global South, Non-Aligned (Yale, 2025) follows the far-flung interwar and postwar networks in which Indian artists and intellectuals such as Francis N. Souza, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore, and Jagdish Swaminathan participated alongside interlocutors like W. E. B. Du Bois, Richard Wright, Octavio Paz, André Malraux, and Le Corbusier in Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - Teacher Organizing Across the Americas: Diverse Strategies for Transforming Unions, Schools, and Society
events.description: Teacher Organizing Across the Americas explores why teachers' unions in Brazil, Mexico, and the United States, representing similar constituencies and fighting for comparable goals, have embraced radically different strategies. Through an ethnographic comparison of teacher organizing in São Paulo, Oaxaca, and New York, the book focuses on three key strategies in teacher organizing—leftist party politics, autonomist politics, and interest group politics—to demonstrate how the strategic choices teachers make matter for both schools and society. In São Paulo, teachers' leftist party politics helped to elect pro-labor presidents five times, with significant social reforms; yet these same politics failed to influence education policy and led to factionalism within the union. In Oaxaca, teachers' autonomous politics led to robust cultural initiatives, an innovative pedagogical proposal, and the capacity to boycott national education reforms. Finally, in many U.S. cities in the 2000s, teachers rejected interest group politics in favor of rank-and-file caucuses that prioritized union-community coalitions and racial justice, which also created new fault lines within the unions and an ambiguous relationship with electoral politics. Teaching Organizing Across the Americas offers important lessons for both scholars and activists interested in transforming institutions like unions to promote more just schools and societies. Rebecca Tarlau is Associate Professor of Education at Stanford University and former Associate Professor of Labor and Employment Relations at Pennsylvania State University, where she was the co-founder of the Consortium for Social Movements and Education Research and Practice. Her ethnographic research focuses on theories of the state and state-society relations; social movements and popular education; Latin American education and development; and labor movements and teachers' work. She is the author of the award-winning Occupying School, Occupying Land: How the Landless Workers Movement Transformed Brazilian Education (OUP, 2019).

events.title: The maintenance of diversity in plant communities: insights from Amazonian forest dynamics and California serptentine annual plants
events.description: Despite centuries of research, many fundamental features of the structure and dynamics of plant communities defy simple explanation. My research group pursues general answers to these questions through integrative approaches that combine community ecology perspectives with insights from functional ecology, floristics and macroecology. Our lab uses a variety of observational, theoretical and experimental approaches, many of them rooted in plant collections and functional trait databases. First, I will share recent projects exploring the dynamics of a large forest plot in the hyperdiverse Ecuadorian Amazon, where we use functional-trait based approaches and novel computational tools to explore the ways in which edaphic specialization, spatial aggregation, and competition dynamics shape one of the most species-rich forests on the planet. Next, I will highlight our recent work in annual plant communities associated with serpentine soils in coastal California, a species-rich system that is ideal for detailed, theoretically-grounded experiments to disentangle mechanisms of species coexistence. Our recent experimental work demonstrates how species trait differences, contrasting responses to spatial and temporal environmental heterogeneity, and complex higher-order interactions combine to shape the diversity of these systems at both local and landscape scales. Finally, I will share insights from my lab's work on continental and global scale patterns of plant diversity, work that is intimately connected to the development of plant trait and occurrence databases. Taken together, these efforts inform our understanding of the mechanisms that drive the fundamental distribution of plant diversity and function across the planet, as well as our predictions of how species and communities will respond to ongoing global change.

events.title: Racist by Design - Two Centuries of U.S. Immigration Control
events.description: About the lecture Award winning historian Kelly Lytle Hernández will be presenting her work, Racist by Design. In it she reveals how generations of lawmakers and law enforcers built the American immigration system to encourage white immigrants while targeting nonwhite migrants for exclusion, punishment, and removal. The goal, often explicitly stated by the system's architects, was to create a permanent caste of undocumented and criminalized workers to provide cheap labor for the American economy. Lytle Hernández calls Racist by Design "an act of sabotage", a book that will expose the blueprints of the system, so it can be dismantled. About Kelly Lytle Hernández Professor Kelly Lytle Hernández holds The Thomas E. Lifka Endowed Chair in History at UCLA. Her major publications are Migra! A History of the U.S. Border Patrol (University of California Press, 2010), City of Inmates: Conquest, Rebellion, and the Rise of Human Caging in Los Angeles (University of North Carolina Press, 2017), and Bad Mexicans: Race, Empire, and Revolution in the Borderlands (W. W. Norton, 2022). Her forthcoming book, Racist by Design: Two Centuries of U.S. Immigration Control, will be published by W. W. Norton in 2026. In 2016, Professor Lytle Hernández established Million Dollar Hoods (MDH), a university-based but community-driven research initiative that maps the fiscal and human costs of mass incarceration in Los Angeles. She served as the MDH director until 2024 and now serves as the initiative's principal advisor. Professor Lytle Hernández is currently a principal investigator for two additional research collaborations: Mapping Deportations, which maps the history of mass deportation from the United States, and Archiving the Age of Mass Incarceration, which preserves a historic cache of LAPD files and documents the impact of policing on LA residents since the 1970s. For her historical and contemporary work, Professor Lytle Hernández's scholarship has been awarded numerous prizes and honors, including a MacArthur "Genius" Fellowship, and she is currently an elected member of the Society of American Historians, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the Pulitzer Prize Board. Meet and mingle before the lecture on November 5 from 3:00 – 4:00 pm at Kvamme Atrium (outside of Banatao Auditorium). Please join us!

events.description: Join us for a screening of Frontline’s new award-winning documentary One in a Million. Filmed over 10 years, it follows Israa’s epic journey from Syria to Germany and back again. She and her family navigate war, exile, and heartbreak in a foreign land, revealing the complexities of the refugee experience. After the film, producer and Frontline Editor-In-Chief Rainey Aronson-Rath will speak with Berkeley Journalism’s Jason Spingarn-Coff and take questions. Snacks will be served in the lobby before the event. RSVP HERE. In September 2015, filmmakers Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes met Israa, an 11-year-old Syrian girl selling cigarettes on a street corner in Turkey, alongside her father, Tarek. The family had fled Aleppo to join the largest movement of people since the Second World War. Together they trekked through Eastern Europe before finding refuge in Germany, where more than one million asylum seekers were registered by the end of that year. For ten years, the filmmakers continued to document Israa’s life as the challenges of integration and cultural adjustment led to family breakdown as Western culture clashed with Syrian traditions. Following the fall of the Assad regime in 2025, the culminates when the filmmakers follow Israa, now a mother herself, back to the ruins of Aleppo as she confronts her own questions of identity and belonging. The film is a Sundance Winner for both the ‘Audience Award: World Cinema Documentary’ and the ‘World Cinema Documentary Directing Award’.

events.title: Composition Colloquium: Julius Dobos
events.location: Morrison Hall Room 125, UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description: TITLE:Spatial Composition: The New Frontier Composers have been using rhythm and melody for thousands of years; harmony for centuries. Musique concrète expanded the use of timbre some 75 years ago. Are we on the verge of another musical disruption? What if, using spatial location and movement as compositional tools, songwriters, composers, and producers not only mixed but composed in and for immersive systems? Can SPACE be considered a new element of music? Do spatial decisions made during the composition phase have an effect on the musical content itself? Do listeners respond differently to spatially composed music than to immersive mixes of non-spatial concepts? How should one approach writing in an immersive environment to yield conceptually novel musical content? Based on his latest research in spatial composition and reflecting the global interest among music professionals in its findings, this presentation and immersive demonstration by composer Julius Dobos explores the use of spatial location and movement in music composition and production.

events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Harold Hwang: Superconductivity in layered nickelates
events.description: Superconductivity in layered nickelates Unconventional superconductivity in proximity to various strongly correlated phases has been a recurring theme in materials as diverse as heavy fermion compounds, cuprates, pnictides, and twisted bilayer graphene. Here we will discuss a growing family of layered nickelate superconductors. The initial discovery of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates was motivated by looking for an electronic analog of the cuprates. Notable aspects are a doping-dependent superconducting dome, strong magnetic fluctuations, and a landscape of unusual normal state properties from which superconductivity emerges. The subsequent discovery of superconductivity in bulk La3Ni2O7 under high pressure is quite intriguing, in that the d-electron configuration is a priori quite different. Recently, we have used epitaxial strain in (La,Pr)3Ni2O7 thin films to stabilize superconductivity at ambient pressure, which has enabled their extend experimental study and development.Bio: Harold Y. Hwang is the Shadi and Omid Farokhzad Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, of Applied Physics (Stanford University), of Photon Science (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory), Senior Fellow of the Precourt Institute for Energy, and Director of the Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. He received a BS in Physics, BS and MS in Electrical Engineering from MIT (1993), and a PhD in Physics from Princeton University (1997). He was formerly a Member of Technical Staff at Bell Laboratories (1996-2003) and on the faculty at the University of Tokyo (2003-2010). His research is in condensed matter and materials physics, with a focus on correlated electrons and emergent phenomena in quantum materials, and heterostructures for energy applications and devices. He is a fellow of the American Physical Society, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and member of the National Academy of Sciences. Recognitions include the MRS Outstanding Young Investigator Award (2005), the IBM Japan Science Prize (Physics, 2008), the Ho-Am Prize (Science, 2013), the Europhysics Prize (2014, with Jochen Mannhart and Jean-Marc Triscone), and the McGroddy Prize (2024).

events.title: Physics Colloquium with Wallace Marshall: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information
events.description: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information Abstract: Cells show a range of complex behaviors which might normally associated with cognition, including basic forms of learning such as habituation. The giant single-celled ciliate Stentor coeruleus is a pond-dwelling organism that attaches to substrates like pond plants and filter feeds by means of a ring of cilia at one end of the cell. Stentor cells can contract in response to mechanical stimulation, an effective escape mechanism but energetically costly. To avoid contracting due to random collision with non-threatening things like algae or pond plants, but still allow contraction when a large predator attacks, Stentor cells use a simple form of learning: when a cell is mechanically stimulated over and over again, it will gradually stop responding, representing a case of habituation. Our goal is to understand how a single cell learns, without a nervous system. We have developed automated devices for applying series of mechanical stimuli under computer control, which we are now using to test predictions of computational models for learning based on known or plausible biochemical mechanisms. Using this approach we have formulated a simplified biochemical model invoking known or suspected processes, which can account for all prior observations as well as new experiments designed to test the model. Based on this framework, we have investigated the molecular pathways involved in learning in Stentor, which suggests a role for CamKII kinase signaling in the learning process. Currently we are using a frequency domain analysis to probe the learning process, and find that the cell acts like a low pass filter with a fractional order transfer function, which provides us with a new way to discriminate among potential learning mechanisms. Biography: Wallace Marshall is Professor of Biochemistry and Biophysics at the University of California San Francisco. A native Long‐Islander, he received his bachelor's degrees in Electrical Engineering and Biochemistry from the State University of New York at Stony Brook, and his Ph.D. in Biochemistry from UC San Francisco, where he studied organization of chromosomes within the nucleus with John Sedat. He then moved to Yale University for postdoctoral studies with Joel Rosenbaum, where he became interested in questions of organelle size control and cell organization, using cilia, flagella, and centrioles as model systems. In 2003, he joined the faculty at UCSF where he continues to study questions of cellular organization in a variety of model organisms including green algae, yeast, ciliates, and mammalian cells. In recent years, his research program has expanded to include cellular engineering and the study of learning and computation in single cells. Dr. Marshall is an elected Fellow of the American Society for Cell Biology, former co‐director of the Physiology summer course at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, and he currently is Director of the Center for Cellular Construction, an NSF Science and Technology Center (STC) devoted to engineering cells and tissues.

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Marc Hillmyer, McKnight Presidential Endowed Chair, University of Minnesota Telechelic polymers for sustainable polyolefins Polyolefins are ubiquitous. They are lightweight, strong, and stable. These features render them useful in countless applications. Unfortunately, these attributes also contribute to the accumulation of persistent plastic waste in the environment. While polyolefins can be mechanically recycled, often this results in an inferior product and is in part the reason that only a small percentage of polyolefin products are effectively recycled. We have embarked on an effort to prepare polyolefins with functional groups at their chain ends. These telechelic polyolefins can be stitched together to form high molar mass plastics and thermosets. By virtue of the synthetic pathway used to make these materials, we generate products that include weak links along the backbones of the polymer chains. These links can be chemically cleaved to quantitatively deconstruct the material and allow for efficient chemical recycling back to the starting telechelic polymers that can be subsequently repolymerized. Our approach takes advantage of a tandem catalysis strategy that is perfectly atom economic and readily scalable. In this lecture I will discuss the preparation of the telechelic polyolefins and their use in the preparation of degradable polyolefin-based plastics and thermosets. I will also report on their materials properties, scalability, and recyclability.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Physical Chemistry Seminar
events.description: John Eiler, Robert P. Sharp Professor of Geology and Geochemistry, CaltechExploring the organic chemistry of the early solar system using molecular isotopic structureOrganic chemistry is ubiquitous across extraterrestrial environments and dominates the processing and delivery of carbon and nitrogen to rocky planetary bodies. Extraterrestrial settings and materials also present the most clearly revealed and diverse collection of constraints on the ways in which 'prebiotic' chemistry takes its first steps towards life. Some of the most detailed and nuanced constraints on this subject come from the laboratory study of the thousands of organic compounds sampled by carbonaceous meteorites and returned samples of asteroids. However, detailed understanding of these materials has been challenging because they may be intimate mixtures of the products of chemistry operating across many settings and processes. I will explore the origin and evolution of early solar system organic materials through application of molecular isotopic structure — the study of the distributions of naturally occurring rare isotopes (D, 13C, 15N, etc.) at scales of individual atomic positions and considering the very rare versions of molecules that contain two or more rare isotopes. These studies were enabled by more than two decades of inventions in mass spectrometry, studies of the chemical physics of previously unexamined isotopic forms of molecules, and applications to meteorites, returned samples, ancient earth materials and their laboratory analogues. The results reveal the long, complex journey of carbon and other volatile materials from synthesis in the interstellar medium, through the early history of the protoplanetary disk and into the 'prebiotic cauldron' of solar system bodies.The Physical Seminar Series is sponsored by the George C. Pimentel lecture fund

events.title: Ilyas Chattha | Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974
events.description: A talk by Ilyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934), Associate Professor of History at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS), on his new book, Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/history/south-asian-history/citizens-traitors-bengali-internment-pakistan-19711974?format=HB&isbn=9781009568241) (Cambridge University Press, 2025). Drawing on previously untapped sources, the book examines Pakistan's internment of thousands of Bengalis after the 1971 war and explains why this history has largely been overlooked.Sadia Saeed (https://www.usfca.edu/faculty/sadia-saeed), Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of San Francisco will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Faculty Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies; Faculty Director, Global Studies and Global Poverty and Practice (https://blumcenter.berkeley.edu/academics/gppminor/), UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Tue, November 10, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKThe breakup of Pakistan in 1971—following a brutal civil war and military defeat by India—remains shrouded in layers of silence, myth, and contested memory. When the war ended, more than 90,000 Pakistani prisoners of war captured in East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, were transferred to Indian custody. In response, Pakistan interned a comparable number of Bengalis living in West Pakistan, treating them as leverage in negotiations for the prisoners' return. Neither group was allowed to go home immediately, creating what became one of the largest episodes of reciprocal mass internment since 1945. Drawing on a wide range of previously untapped sources, this book reconstructs the resulting crisis of captivity. It traces how Bengalis in West Pakistan were stripped of meaningful citizenship and recast as "traitors" and "enemies" in the aftermath of the Bangladesh War. More than half a century later, their internment remains largely absent from accounts of the most consequential political crisis in Pakistan's history. By recovering this neglected history, the book not only reveals the human and political consequences of mass detention but also explains how—and why—the experience of interned Bengalis was erased from the historical record. SPEAKER BIOIlyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934) is Associate Professor of History at Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) and a historian of modern South Asia. Educated at the universities of Warwick and Southampton in the United Kingdom, he has previously been affiliated with the Centre for Imperial and Post-Colonial Studies at the University of Southampton, the University of Warwick, and SOAS University of London. Dr Chattha's research focuses on late colonial Punjab, Partition, migration, borders and borderlands, collective violence, and the formation of the early postcolonial Pakistani state. He has written extensively on the long-term consequences of the partitions of 1947 and 1971, with particular attention to displacement, citizenship, internment, property, and state-building. He is the author of Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (Cambridge University Press, 2025), which examines the wartime and postwar experiences of Bengalis interned in West Pakistan; The Punjab Borderland: Mobility, Materiality and Militancy, 1947–1987 (Cambridge University Press, 2022); and Partition and Locality: Violence, Migration and Development in Gujranwala and Sialkot, 1947–1961 (Oxford University Press, 2012). His current book project explores the history of evacuee and enemy property in Pakistan.EVENT POSTER TBA _____________ Established in 2013 with a generous gift from the Subir & Malini Chowdhury Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subir_Chowdhury), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (https://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/) at UC Berkeley champions the study of Bangladesh's cultures, peoples and history. The first of its kind in the US, the Center's mission is to create an innovative model combining research, scholarships, the promotion of art and culture, and the building of ties between institutions in Bangladesh and the University of California. events.title: Under Pressure: Attitudes Towards China Among American Foreign Policy Professionals | Lecture by Rory Truex
events.description: How do social norms and professional incentives affect policy discourse within the Washington foreign policy community? We conducted over 50 semi-structured interviews and a survey of nearly five-hundred American foreign policy and national security professionals about their views towards the People's Republic of China. Over one fifth of survey respondents noted instances of professional pressure to voice a more hawkish point of view towards China, and many feared being perceived as naive or compromised by their views on, ties to, and experiences in China. These pressures were particularly acute for foreign policy professionals that are traditionally marginalized from power–those who are younger, non-white, or female. Our interview subjects reported a number of different coping strategies, including trying to communicate their views in the language of the perceived consensus. This "discourse mirroring" is distinct from preference falsification and self-censorship but may still contribute to difficulties in gauging peoples' true attitudes. Speaker BioRory Truex is Associate Professor of Politics and International Affairs at Princeton, where his research and teaching focuses on authoritarianism. He is the host of Civic Forum, a podcast about the big questions facing democracy, in the US and elsewhere.

Talk Summary: This talk will introduce Hannah Shepherd's new book, The Narrowing Sea, via vignettes of the imperial region that developed across the Tsushima Straits between Pusan and Fukuoka in the seven decades from 1876 to 1953. It will offer the imperial region as a useful scale of analysis and connection between other imperial histories, and connect the urbanization of the imperial era with contemporary Japan's urban issues, before ending with a glimpse of new work that continues some of the histories and legacies discussed in The Narrowing Sea. Speaker Bio: Hannah Shepherd is Assistant Professor in the Department of History at Yale University. She received her Ph.D. in History from Harvard University. Before joining the Yale faculty, she was Junior Research Fellow in History at Trinity College, University of Cambridge. At Yale, Shepherd teaches courses on modern Japanese history, Korea and the Japanese Empire, and the history of colonial and imperial cities. Her book, The Narrowing Sea: Fukuoka, Pusan, and the Rise and Fall of an Imperial Region, came out in December 2025, from University of California Press. With Amy Stanley, she is currently working on co-translating and co-editing an English memoir of a former comfort woman, with the working title, The Life of Mun Ok Chu: a Korean woman's story of war and empire.

events.title: Laurent Warlouzet | Liberty, Solidarity and Community: Capitalism and European Integration, 1945 to the Present
events.description: How have European countries coped with the challenge of industrial capitalism and the rise of superpowers? Through an analysis of European integration from 1945 to the present day, Laurent Warlouzet argues that the European response was to create both new institutions, in particular the European Union, and an original framework of governance for capitalism. Beyond the European case, he demonstrates that capitalism is not just a contest between free marketeers and their opponents, those in favour of welfare and environmental policies, because there is a third camp that defends protectionism and assertive defence policies. Hence, the governance of capitalism has three foundational principles– liberty, solidarity, and community. The book explores debates among Europeans about how to address global interdependence in political, economic, and environmental terms. It is based on fresh archival evidence collected in eight countries. Laurent Warlouzet is professor of history at Paris Sorbonne Université. A former postdoctoral fellow at the London School of Economics (LSE) and at the European University Institute (EUI), he works on the international economic history of the post-1919 period, particularly European integration and comparative European history. His previous monograph in English (Governing Europe in a Globalizing World, 2018) was reviewed in Foreign Affairs. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Capitalism. European integration and capitalism is an updated version of Europe contre Europe, originally published in French and reviewed in the mainstream media, including Le Monde, Le Grand Continent and Mediapart. The book will be published in German by Hamburger and in Italian by Luiss UP. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Community is available in open-access on the Cambridge UP here (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/liberty-solidarity-and-community/355531CFEE184AFF8B706B24D25EC368).
