events.title: Composition Colloquium: Andrea Agostini
events.location: Morrison Hall Room 125, UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description: Andrea Agostini was born on 21 May 1975 in Bologna, Italy. He studied at the Conservatorio Giovanni Battista Martini, where he received a degree in composition in 2000 (studying under Alessandro Solbiati, Giovanni Verrando, and Paolo Aralla), in electronic music in 2001 (studying with Lelio Camilleri), and piano in 2004. Between 1999 and 2006, he also took masterclasses with Ivan Fedele, Brian Ferneyhough, Michael Jarrell, and François Paris. In 2008-2010, he completed his studies with the Cursus (IRCAM's composition and computer music course). He was an IRCAM scholar-in-residence from 2011 to 2013. Andrea Agostini composes instrumental and electroacoustic music, for which he has won numerous prizes and awards, including the Zucchelli Prize in 1999 and in 2000, and the Magone Award in 2001. In 2002, he was a finalist for the Prix international Noroit-Léonce Petitot. In 2003, he won the Concurso Internacional de Composição Electroacústica Música Viva. In 2005 he received third prize for composition in the Seoul International Music Competition and an honorable mention at the Gaudeamus Festival Composers Awards. In 2007 he was a finalist in the Franco Evangelisti International Composition, sponsored by Nuovo Consonanza, and received a Commande d'état (a commission from the French Ministry of Culture) for Musica per il chiostro di Royaumont. His music is performed in festivals across the world, including Festival Musica in Strasbourg, MiTo and Sincronie in Milan, REC in Emilia-Romagna, the IMEB Festival in Bourges, Festival MIA in Annecy, and Northern Spark in Minneapolis. His curiosity for different musical languages led him to explore rock and improvisation, and to study non-Western musical practices. He plays bass with the rock band Frida X, for which he is also an arranger, progammer, and sound engineer. He also composes music for theater, cinema, and radio, and live electronics and motion capture for Project C, a group specialized in sound design for theater performances. He also designs sound environments for visual art installations. With Daniele Ghisi, he created a digital platform for computer-aided composition titled "bach: automated composer's helper". In 2017, during his research residency at IRCAM, he developed a programming language for the Max environment, creating a set of tools based on the bach library. As a musician, Andrea Agostini has collaborated with ensembles such as Icarus and the Orchestre national de la RAI in Turin, for concerts and recordings of works by Fausto Romitelli, Giovanni Verrando, and Oscar Bianchi. In addition, he has given masterclasses and workshops in the conservatories of Bologna, Genoa, and Strasbourg, and in several universities in the United States (Harvard, San Diego, and Stanford). He is currently professor of computer music (algorithmic and computer-aided composition) at the Conservatory of Turin. NOTE: Andrea is in residence at CNMAT for the Fall semester

events.description: "Unsilencing the Archive: Enunciation, Song, and Romani History" Dr. Ioanida Costache, Stanford University Abstract: This talk explores the silence of the archive and its attendant epistemic regimes in relation to Romani people, who have served as an "Ontological Other" in the European imaginary (Wynter 1987). I posit that archival silence registers the racialization that undergirds systems of knowledge production and ask: How might sound "augment" a Romani subjectivity conditioned by abjection? At stake is music's capacity to function as an affective archive and alternative site of historical enunciation. Bio: Ioanida Costache is Assistant Professor of Ethnomusicology and, by courtesy, of Anthropology at Stanford University. She is also a faculty affiliate of the Center for Comparative Studies in Race and Ethnicity. Her work explores the legacies of Romani historical trauma and feminist critiques of the present inscribed in Romani music, sound, and art. Her writing has been published in EuropeNow, Revista ARTA, Critical Romani Studies, and European History Quarterly and is forthcoming in Ethnomusicology. Her research has been supported by two Fulbright grants and the Council for European Studies. She has held visiting and postdoctoral fellowships at the University of Pennsylvania, the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and the USC Shoah Foundation. A reception will follow.

events.title: The 2026 Emilio Segrè Lecture Featuring Francis Halzen: ICECUBE: Opening a Neutrino Window on the Universe from the South Pole
events.location: The Chevron Auditorium at International House
events.description: ICECUBE: Opening a Neutrino Window on the Universe from the South PoleFrancis Halzen, University of Wisconsin–Madison Abstract: The IceCube project at the South Pole melted 86 holes 2.5 kilometer deep in the Antarctic ice sheet to construct an enormous astronomical observatory that is also the largest neutrino detector ever built. The experiment discovered a flux of neutrinos from deep space with energies more than a million times those of neutrinos produced at accelerator laboratories like Fermilab. Some originate in the enigmatic cosmic particle accelerators that are the sources of cosmic rays. This lecture will discuss the IceCube neutrino telescope and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of cosmic origin. It will highlight the recent discovery that high-energy neutrinos—and cosmic rays—originate in sources powered by rotating supermassive black holes in active galaxies. With gravitational waves, high-energy gamma rays and neutrinos, IceCube launched multiparticle astronomy. Francis Halzen is a Vilas and Gregory Breit Distinguished Professor of Physics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Born in Belgium, Halzen received his Master's and PhD degrees from the KU-Leuven, Belgium, and has been on the physics faculty at UW–Madison since 1972; in 2021, Halzen was named a Vilas Research Professor, one of the university's most prestigious honors. He has been a fellow of the American Physical Society since 1994 and a member of the US National Academy since 2024, and is the recipient of numerous awards, including the 2014 Smithsonian American Ingenuity Award, the 2015 Balzan Prize, a 2018 Bruno Pontecorvo Prize, the 2019 IUPAP Yodh Prize, the 2021 Bruno Rossi Prize, the 2021 Homi Bhabha Award, and honorary doctorates at several universities. Halzen is the Principal Investigator of IceCube, a cubic-kilometer neutrino telescope buried in the Antarctic ice at the South Pole. IceCube's first observations of high-energy cosmic neutrinos garnered the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award. In September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from the direction of a blazar called TXS 0506+056. This was the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since they were discovered over one hundred years ago. Also a skilled science communicator, Halzen travels widely, giving about 20 or more invited talks per year at conferences, workshops, and colloquia. He also gives regular public talks to local and national groups and interviews for television and radio. Halzen is the co-author of Quarks and Leptons, a classic textbook on modern particle physics that continues to be used extensively throughout college campuses today. He has a large number of publications to his credit and has written or edited several other books. His essay "Antarctic Dreams," about the early days of AMANDA, IceCube's precursor, was featured in The Best American Science Writing 2000.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Founders and Their Heterogeneous Firms"
events.description: Abstract: Firm creation is at the heart of macroeconomic growth, but entrepreneurial outcomes are highly unequal. In this paper, we study the determinants of which entrants become large firms with macroeconomic importance. Using employer-employee-shareholder linked Canadian administrative data based on tax records, we find that workers with higher employment earnings are more likely both to enter entrepreneurship and to found larger firms with greater growth potential. We incorporate this link between founders' labor-market and entrepreneurial capacities into a quantitative model of endogenous occupational choice. In the presence of ex-ante heterogeneity, small business tax deductions induce negative selection by drawing lower-potential entrepreneurs into entry, largely oﬀsetting their positive eﬀects in alleviating financial frictions and generating a quantity-quality trade-oﬀ in the design of entrepreneurial policies.

events.title: Bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā - Not a moonless night: Śamathadeva's Upāyikā, the oral life of Mūlasarvāstivāda scripture, and early Buddhist philology
events.description: An exposition of the Abhidharma without the Āgamas, however flawless, "does not capture the heart, just like a moonless night." So runs the colophon of Śamathadeva's Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā (Upāyikā for short), a monumental Sanskrit commentary now extant only in Tibetan translation. The Upāyikā is a commentary of an unusual kind. Rather than explaining Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya through standard exegetical procedures, it traces its scriptural citations back to their authoritative canonical settings in the Āgamas, often reproducing extensive passages, some of which do not otherwise survive in the received corpora. The same colophon states that these canonical materials were recalled from memory. Taking this seriously, the lecture will treat the Upāyikā both as a companion reader to the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya and as a witness to the oral textual life of the contemporaneous Mūlasarvāstivāda lineages of recitation in India. It will examine how the scriptures available to Śamathadeva were organized and transmitted, and will try to locate the otherwise unknown figure of Śamathadeva in time and space. Close philological engagement with this text will show what the practice of early Buddhist philology has to say about what counts as a text and as text-historical evidence.Bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā is a Visiting Associate Research Professor in the Department of Buddhist Sudies at Dharma Drum Institute of Liberal Arts (Taiwan), Director of the Āgama Research Group, and currently the Numata Visiting Professor for Buddhist Studies at the University of California at Berkeley. link (https://bhikkhunidhammadinna.com/)

events.title: Talk by Aditya Balasubramanian (Title TBD)
events.description: A talk by Aditya Balasubramanian (https://researchers.anu.edu.au/researchers/balasubramanian-a), Senior Lecturer in History at the Australian National University. Event moderated by Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, Nov 17, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–About the Speaker:Aditya Balasubramanian (https://researchers.anu.edu.au/researchers/balasubramanian-a) is a Senior Lecturer at ANU's School of History, in the College of Arts and Social Sciences (CASS). Aditya's first book, Toward a Free Economy: Swatantra and Opposition Politics in Democratic India (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2023), is a history of economic ideas and politics (UK/US link (https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691205243/toward-a-free-economy) South Asia link (https://www.amazon.in/Toward-Free-Economy-Swatantra-Opposition/dp/0691256578)). It was shortlisted for the 2022 Elder Prize in the Social Sciences of the American Institute of Indian Studies and the 2024 W.K. Hancock Prize for best first monograph of the Australian Historical Association, and longlisted for the 2024 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay Prize of the New India Foundation. A suite of peer-reviewed articles published over the last several years have interrogated various aspects of Indian political economy between the 1940s and the 1970s. Topics range from India's role in the international economic order, famine in Travancore during World War II, Hindu nationalist economic thought and policy, and anticorruption. He is currently working on two projects. The first is an environmental and economic history of roadbuilding and transport in India. Initial thoughts appeared in this post (https://histecon.fas.harvard.edu/climate-loss/roads/index.html) for the Harvard Center for History and Economics' "Visualizing Climate and Loss" blog in October 2023. During 2025-2028, he is the recipient of an Australian Research Council Discovery Early Career Research Award (DECRA) for this project. The second is a synthetic history of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy of 1984, the world's largest industrial disaster. This project is especially concerned with failures of relief and rehabilitation, chronic illnesses, and ongoing environmental pollution. He has just completed an article on forest management in India and is working on an article that sketches a revisionist history of migration between South and Southeast Asia. At ANU, Aditya teaches or has taught historical methods, environmental history, the history of political economy, and South Asian history. His teaching has been recognized with nominations for College and University-wide prizes. He is the Deputy Director of ANU's Center for Environmental History (https://history.cass.anu.edu.au/centres/ceh) and founded the ANU Capitalism Studies Network (http://csn.anu.edu.au/) with Will Bateman (Law) and Melinda Cooper (Sociology). He is completing a second term as Board Member of the South Asia Research Institute (2020-2021, 2024-6). From 2018 to 2024, he created and coordinated the Archives of Economic Life in South and Southeast Asia (https://www.histecon.magd.cam.ac.uk/archives-asia/index.html) website (you can learn more about it in this (https://toynbeeprize.org/posts/doing-online-south-southeast-asian-history/) Toynbee Prize Blog interview). _________________ Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952).PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking is not always easily available in Berkeley. events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Ignacio Navarrete
events.description: In Sneaking into Print (Toronto, 2026), Ignacio Navarrete (Spanish & Portuguese) explores the impact of early printing on narrative literature in Spain. He reveals how new technology enabled older texts and translations to circulate alongside newly written works, giving rise to a distinct narrative culture. Through an in-depth study of various narrative subgenres including hagiography, the epic, and sentimental fiction, Sneaking into Print integrates historical bibliography, material book features, and literary analysis. By examining texts as physical artifacts and narrative constructs, the book sheds light on their broader implications for narrative theory, offering fresh perspectives on the intersections of literature, materiality, and the early print marketplace. Navarrete is joined by Nicholas Paige (French). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: International Court of Justice: Judicial Fellowship Panel
events.description: ICJ Judicial Fellowship Panel Wednesday, November 18 · 1:00 PM · Berkeley Law, Room 141 Each year, the International Court of Justice selects fifteen Judicial Fellows from hundreds of candidates nominated by law schools around the world to clerk at the Peace Palace in The Hague for ten months. Berkeley Law nominates up to four candidates each year and provides a significant fellowship stipend for any Berkeley nominee the Court selects. Join BJIL and ILS, with support from the Miller Institute, for a conversation with four recent Judicial Fellows: Félix Aguettant (Berkeley Law LL.M. ’23), Allyson Ping, Lara Manbeck, and Marina Wilbraham. They will talk about the application process, their time at the Court, and where the fellowship has taken them since. PANELISTS Félix Aguettant is a lawyer in the Legal Service of the European Commission, in the EU External Relations and International Law team, based in Brussels. He is also a PhD candidate in public international law at the Sorbonne. He was a 2024-25 Judicial Fellow for H.E. Judge Abraham and H.E. President Iwasawa. He is an alumnus of Berkeley Law’s executive LLM program and was nominated to the fellowship by Berkeley Law in 2024. He is currently the head coach of Berkeley Law’s 2026-27 Jessup team. Félix is bilingual in English and French and is a member of the California Bar. To date, Felix is the only Berkeley Law alum to have ever been a judicial fellow! Allyson Ping is a litigation associate at Debevoise & Plimpton, New York. From 2024-2025, she served as a Judicial Fellow to H.E. President Iwasawa Yuji. Allyson received a J.D. from Columbia Law School in 2024, where she was a member of the Jessup Moot Court team and was co-Executive Editor of the Columbia Journal of Transnational Law. Lara Manbeck is an Associate at Covington & Burling in Washington, D.C. From 2025 to 2026, she served as a Judicial Fellow to H.E. Judge Nolte and later as an Associate Legal Officer at the Court. She received her J.D. from Columbia Law School, where she served as Editor-in-Chief of the Columbia Journal of Transnational Law, an MPhil from the University of Cambridge, and a B.A. from New York University. Prior to law school, she worked in the Office of the Director-General of the International Development Law Organization. Marina Wilbraham is currently a Law Clerk at White and Case LLP, in the firm’s LA office, where her practice focuses on international technology disputes. She was a 2025-2026 Judicial Fellow for H.E. Judge Sarah H. Cleveland. Previously, she was an Associate at Debevoise & Plimpton LLP for two years in New York, in the Litigation Department, where she worked on a mix of international arbitration, public international law, and commercial litigation matters. Marina is a 2023 Yale Law School graduate. BERKELEY LAW’S JUDICIAL FELLOWSHIP APPLICATIONS Applications for the 2027–28 judicial fellowship, run by the CDO, will open in December 2026 and close in January 2027. Details about the 2026-27 application for Berkeley Law’s nomination process here. You can find details about the fellowship on the ICJ Judicial Fellowship website. JD and LL.M. students in the classes of 2025, 2026 and 2027 are eligible to apply, provided they meet other eligibility criteria of the Court. LUNCH Lunch will be provided if you RSVP here.

events.title: Dylan Spaulding: The US Nuclear Paradigm Shift: Pit Production, Nuclear Testing, and the fate of Stockpile Stewardship
events.description: Events Add to Calendar iCal / Outlook The US nuclear weapons complex is undergoing its biggest transformation since the end of the Cold War. Increasingly sophisticated experimental, computational, and manufacturing techniques that emerged to support a strategy of science-based stockpile stewardship are now being applied as tools for vertical proliferation as emphasis shifts from ‘stewardship’ to production. The evolution of laboratory tools for weapons development comes with both challenges and opportunities for verification, nonproliferation, and disarmament. This talk will address the paradigm shift underway in the US and its implications for new plutonium pit production and the potential resumption of nuclear testing.

events.description: The Bancroft Library holds the world's largest collection of George Sterling manuscripts, photographs, books, and biographical and critical materials. During the first quarter of the 20th century, Sterling was one of the most acclaimed poets in the U.S. Across his career, he wrote songs, plays, movies, short stories, essays, and more than a thousand poems. His works were published in many American literary magazines, in more than a hundred newspapers, in anthologies, and in his own books. To mark the 100th anniversary of his death, foremost Sterling experts S.T. Joshi, Ariadna García Carreño, and Vince Emery will reveal rarities that tell the surprising story of the poet and playwright.

events.title: Esha Niyogi De | Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia
events.description: A talk by Esha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/), Senior Lecturer in UCLA's Writing Programs, on her new book, Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=p088285) (University of Illinois Press, December 2024). The book uncovers the overlooked histories of women who worked as producers, directors, performers, and "star-authors" across the film industries of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. De examines how these women used stardom, collaboration, and creative labor to cross geographic, institutional, and gendered boundaries, claim greater authority over filmmaking, and challenge the structures that often obscured their contributions to South Asian cinema. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Thu, November 19, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOK This book talk delves into previously submerged histories and hidden voices of women directors and film entrepreneurs from Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India. Drawing on neglected archives and rare field interviews with filmmakers and fans, Esha tells a comparative story of women's creative authority and entrepreneurial labor in selected film industries of South Asia��industries and markets that share languages, arts, and geopolitical rifts. Using "transborder" to refer not only to territorial borders but also to institutional and conceptual ones, her story dwells on two eras of women's cinema in this postcolonial region. In the era of the "star-authors" (50s-90s), female stars in Dhaka, Lahore, and Kolkata perform personas ambiguously to access infrastructures and direct fiction films that breach sexual and national borders. In the era of the "woman director" (2000s), even though opportunities appear to burgeon across the region, women negotiate transnational borders that take less obvious forms of brand-making and censorship. The talk will include rare footage from fiction films made by Kohinoor Akhtar Suchanda, Babita, Nargis Akhter (Bangladesh), Shamim Ara (Pakistan), and Kanan Devi (India). SPEAKER BIOEsha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/)'s research interests lie in South Asian gender politics, film and performance history, and literary history. She is the author of two monographs, a recent study of women's cinemas in selected film industries of Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India titled Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (University of Illinois Press, 2024), and an earlier book on sexual politics and postcoloniality in literature, cinema, and choreography in the Bengal region titled Empire, Media, and the Autonomous Woman: A Feminist Critique of Postcolonial Thought (Oxford University Press, 2011). Other publications include two co-edited books, from University of Washington Press and Duke University Press, and many articles. She is working on two new book projects. The first, a study of the renowned Pakistani actress-singer and film director Noor Jehan in relation to Muslim nationalist arts in the mid-twentieth century, is titled Recasting Noor Jehan:Melody Queen, Film Pioneer, and the Making of National Cultures in South Asia (co-authored with Gwendolyn Sarah Kirk). The second, a comparative study of gendered choreographies of protest in twentieth century avant-garde and industrial films, made by Zahir Raihan, Satyajit Ray, Rangeela, among others, is tentatively titled Moving Bodies Out of Line: Filmic Choreographies, Protest Movements, and Queerness in South Asian Cinemas. Esha is a Senior Lecturer in the Division of Writing Programs at UCLA and a Faculty Affiliate of the UCLA Center for India and South Asia.EVENT POSTER TBA _____________ Established in 2013 with a generous gift from the Subir & Malini Chowdhury Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subir_Chowdhury), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (https://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/) at UC Berkeley champions the study of Bangladesh's cultures, peoples and history. The first of its kind in the US, the Center's mission is to create an innovative model combining research, scholarships, the promotion of art and culture, and the building of ties between institutions in Bangladesh and the University of California. Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/The-Subir-Malini-Chowdhury-Center-for-Bangladesh-Studies-752426458213022/?ref=hl) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952).PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking is not always easily available in Berkeley. events.title: Earl L. Muetterties Lectures in Chemistry
events.description: Joesp Cornella, Director, Max-Plank InstituteExploring the Far Reaches of the Periodic Table: Bismuth Redox CatalysisThe success of transition metal catalysis in organic synthesis is rooted in decades of advances in fundamental organometallic reactivity. Bonding theory on d-block elements has allowed synthetic chemists to design novel and powerful catalysts that underpin modern chemical manufacturing. However, the increasing demand, cost, and environmental impact associated with many transition metals highlighted the need for alternatives. To this end, exploration of underutilized regions of the periodic table might reveal unconventional mechanisms inaccessible within established frameworks, making the search for sustainable alternatives a powerful driver of discovery. Beyond the transition metal realm lies a group of elements that have largely been overlooked by the synthetic community: the heavy elements, ignored by many due to the historically bad reputation associated to them. Yet, among them, one can find bismuth (Bi), placed at the fringe of the periodic table, virtually representing the last stable element. Bismuth is the main character of this talk, which will highlight how our laboratory unlocked its potential as redox catalyst for organic synthesis. Importantly, we will discuss how relativistic effects encoded in bismuth's electronic structure are the main driver in certain contexts, thus shaping the kinetic and thermodynamic landscapes of chemical reactions.Lecture 2 of 2

events.description: A cornerstone of the department's season, student performers join Gamelan Sari Raras and take the stage under the lead of longtime ensemble director Midiyanto. This intricate ensemble art form—which famously inspired the impressionist harmonies of 19th-century Western composers—continues to bridge the divide of global music. For the Fall semester, the ensemble will explore gamelan's past and present through traditional compositions, innovative new works by Midiyanto, the transcendent vocal styling of Heni Savitri, and the stately elegance of classical court dance by Lestari Indonesia (directed by Ninik Lunde). events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Samuel Gurrola Viramontes, CIMAT GuanajatoIn this talk, within the framework of real infinitesimal free probability introduced by Cebron and Mingo, we will discuss the calculation of the real infinitesimal free cumulants of independent complex Wigner matrices. Our approach relies on establishing a combinatorial relation between annular non-crossing partitions and families of directed graphs. As a consequence, we show that independent complex Wigner matrices are asymptotically real infinitesimally free. In particular, under mild conditions, a complex Wigner matrix is asymptotically infinitesimally free from its transpose. This is based on joint work with James A. Mingo (arXiv:2609.24023).

events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Amy Weeks, Assistant Professor, University of Wisconsin, MadisonNew enzyme chemistry to decipher post-translational modification function Spatial organization and temporal dynamics are essential properties of cellular signaling. Post-translational modifications (PTMs) to proteins relay biological signals by exerting precise spatiotemporal control over protein function, localization, and lifetime. A systems-level experimental map of post-translationally modified proteins across subcellular space and time would transform our understanding of how PTMs orchestrate complex cellular functions in response to biological stimuli. However, such a map is inaccessible with current technologies. To meet this challenge, the Weeks lab is focused on developing new chemical and enzymatic tools for PTM proteomics with subcellular spatial and temporal resolution. We develop chemical probes and genetically targetable, PTM-selective proximity labeling enzymes to covalently tag post-translationally modified proteins in specific subcellular locations, enabling their enrichment and analysis with mass spectrometry-based proteomics experiments. We focus on two pervasive PTMs, proteolysis and phosphorylation, both of which play critical roles in myriad biological signaling pathways relevant to human health and disease. Our technologies are broadly applicable to a wide variety of protease and kinase signaling pathways and provide an integrated view of cellular signaling with implications for both fundamental biological discovery and therapeutic innovation.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

Her first book, Every Man's Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism (Princeton University Press, 2026), examines how a sovereign conception of the white patriarchal family was at the crux of an emerging conservative ideology opposed to the modern liberal state. The book is an extended version of her dissertation, which was awarded the 2019 Lerner-Scott Prize for the best dissertation in US women's history by the Organization of American Historians. She has held fellowships from the Jefferson Scholars Foundation, the Institute of Citizens and Scholars (formerly the Woodrow Wilson Institute), and, prior to joining the University of Melbourne, was an assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong. She is now researching a project on the gendered politics of alternative health movements, including anti-vaccination, anti-fluoridation, and home birth movements, in the twentieth-century United States. *If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) to fully participate in this event, please contact Ariana Ceja at centerrg@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Importing Aggregate Demand"
events.description: Abstract: How exposed are open economies to global demand shocks? In equilibrium, foreign booms can be absorbed either by domestic consumption ("quantities") or by real exchange rate appreciation ("prices"). We show that failures of Ricardian equivalence and global financial market imperfections, two frictions popular in much recent work, have opposite effects on the split: while elevated marginal propensities to consume push towards quantities, financial frictions instead increase price adjustment. As the flexible-price equilibrium generally features a mix of quantity and price responses, policy needs to be contractionary to achieve flexible-price outcomes if the spending effect dominates, and vice-versa if financial frictions are severe. In our quantitative explorations the spending effect tends to win the race, necessitating aggressive domestic policy action.

events.title: 2026 Berkeley Bioengineering Distinguished Lecture with Clifford Brangwynne, PhD
events.description: Fluid Machinery: The Nucleolus, Ribosomes, and Aging Abstract: Research combining insights from materials physics and cell biology has ushered in a new paradigm for understanding how the chaotic intracellular environment is brought to order, through the collective condensation of biomolecules into droplets of living information. In this talk, I will present an overview of these principles and ongoing work in this field, with a particular emphasis on the interplay between liquid-like condensates and traditional biomolecular machines, such as the ribosome, which forms through a complex assembly process in the multiphase nucleolus. Our lab has recently developed a set of tools to probe and engineer the nucleolus and the production of ribosomes, as well as their cytoplasmic function in protein translation. These studies are yielding new insights into how assembled ribosomes function in space and time, and how ribosomes can become dysregulated by molecular and organismal aging.

Talk Summary: The rise of the illiberal, far-right politics threatens democratic system throughout the world. The South Korean president Yoon Seok-yeol's martial law declaration in December 2024 stunned the world. More puzzling is that Yoon's insurrection unexpectedly gained substantial support from the ruling right-wing party and ordinary citizens. Why do ordinary citizens support authoritarian leaders and martial law in a democratic country? What draws these citizens to extreme actions and ideas? Through eighteen months of field research and drawing from rich qualitative data, this talk will provide an in-depth account of the ideas and practices of the far-right groups and organizations, and help to understand the roots of current democratic regression. Speaker Bio: Myungji Yang is Professor of Sociology at the University of Hawai'i-Mānoa. A political sociologist and social movement scholar, she is interested in the issues of power, inequality, civil society and democracy. Her research has appeared in Nations and Nationalism, Politics and Society, Mobilization: An International Inquiry, Urban Studies, and Sociological Inquiry, among other venues. She is the author of two books, From Miracle to Mirage (2018, Cornell University Press) and Reactionary Politics in South Korea: Historical Legacies, Far-Right Intellectuals, and Political Mobilization (2026, Cambridge University Press). She is currently developing a research project on young men's radicalization and anti-feminist politics.

events.title: Inorganic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Stefan Minasian, Staff Chemist, LBNLThe Counterintuitive Relationship between Orbital Energy, Orbital Overlap,and Covalency in f-Element Molecules Why are some metal–ligand bonds more covalent than others? Typically, chemists invoke two factors: how well the metal and ligand orbitals overlap in space, and how closely their energies match. Yet these contributions have been surprisingly difficult to separate, by either experiment or theory. This lecture will describe how ligand K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), combined with high-level spectral simulations, can measure both. Comparisons of isostructural fluoride and chloride complexes of transition metals (Ti, Zr, Hf), lanthanides (Ce), and actinides (U, Np, Pu) show that the two factors often work against each other. Greater orbital overlap does not necessarily produce a more covalent bond, and the balance between overlap and energy matching depends on the metal and on the symmetry of the interaction. These results also provide experimental benchmarks against which computational descriptions of bonding can be tested. The second part of the lecture will extend this approach to organometallic lanthanide complexes, probed using carbon K-edge XAS. In molecules such as cerocene, Ce(C8H8)2, and Cp′3Eu, the ground state cannot be described by a single electronic configuration. In these systems, the 4f orbital mixing observed by X-ray spectroscopy also appears as partial charge transfer from the ligands to the metal. Relating these two descriptions shows how 4f electrons can participate in bonding while remaining largely localized, and how 4f covalency can shape physical properties such as magnetic susceptibility. This leads to broader questions about how covalency and multiconfigurational ground states are connected across the f-block.The Inorganic Seminar Series is sponsored by Earl L. Muetterties lecture fund

events.description: RSVP to get the Zoom linkThis workshop will help you navigate the legal and practical questions that AI tools raise for academic authors. We'll cover how using generative AI in your research and writing can affect your copyright and authorship, what current publisher and journal policies require you to disclose, and how AI training on scholarly work intersects with your rights as an author. events.title: Rhiju Das: "De novo design of RNA with deep learning"
events.description: RNA design has long been limited by the accuracy of RNA structure prediction. I will describe how the video game Eterna has elicited modeling and design tools for previously intractable pseudoknotted folds, multi-state sensors for disease states, and polymerase ribozymes that copy RNA. AI teams now work alongside Eterna players, and both are scored by prospective high-throughput experiments. Under that pressure, RNA design is improving quickly.

events.title: Lunch Poems: Bianca Stone
events.description: Lunch Poems (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/lunch-poems), Berkeley's storied noontime poetry series, welcomes Bianca Stone. Bianca Stone is the author of four collections of poetry. Her three most recent, all from Tin House Books, are The Near and Distant World (2026); What Is Otherwise Infinite (2022), winner of the 2022 Vermont Book Award; and The Möbius Strip Club of Grief (2018). Her work has appeared widely in such magazines as The New Yorker, The Atlantic, and Poetry. She is a visiting lecturer in poetry at Dartmouth College and teaches classes on poetry and poetic study at the Ruth Stone House in Goshen, Vermont, where she hosts the Ode & Psyche Podcast. Stone is currently serving as the poet laureate of Vermont (2024-28). The Lunch Poems series, founded by Professor Robert Hass, is supported by Dr. and Mrs. Tom Colby, the UC Berkeley Library, the Morrison Library Fund, the UC Berkeley English Department, and the Deans' Office of the College of Letters & Science. events.title: 2027 Sheng Yen Conference
events.description: The scholastic traditions associated with Sarvāstivāda and the Abhidharma corpus more broadly were transmitted to China beginning in the fourth and fifth centuries and became a significant focus of translation activity under the direction of Xuanzang in the seventh century. Yet modern scholarship often assumes that Chinese Buddhist scholiasts had little sustained interest in, or use for, Abhidharma. According to this view, Abhidharma was dismissed as "Hīnayāna" and overshadowed by the rise of indigenous Chinese Buddhist traditions such as Chan, Tiantai, and Huayan. There is, however, ample evidence that Abhidharma continued to be studied and valued by Chinese exegetes irrespective of their doctrinal or school affiliation, and that it retained an important place in monastic curricula from the medieval period down to the present day. This conference seeks to reconsider the reception and enduring influence of Abhidharma in Chinese Buddhism.Titles, Abstracts, and Bios. (https://events.berkeley.edu/live/files/69-titles-abstracts-and-bios-1pdf)Friday 2:30-5:30 pmAbhidharma Learning in China Chair: Alexander von Rospatt Eric Greene (Yale University): "Abhidharma Methodology in the First Era of Chinese Buddhist Scholasticism." Hou Xiaoming (Ghent University): "A Curriculum in Diagram: Dunhuang Path Charts and the Teaching of Abhidharma." Patrick Magoffin (Postdoctoral Fellow, UC Berkeley): "Interpreting and Teaching the Lengyan jing: A Conduit for Abhidharmic Learning and Textual Practices in the Song (960–1279)."Saturday 9:30 to 12:30 pmChinese Exegesis I Chair: Jacob Dalton Lu Huang (UC Berkeley): "Views of Pre-Xuanzang Abhidharma Masters as Preserved in the Jushe lun ji." Howard Mu (UC Berkeley): "Shentai's Interpretative Approach: Some General Features of the Jushe lunshu 俱舍論疏." Lin Xueni (University of Heidelberg): "A New Understanding of Dharmas: The Concept of shifa (實法) in the *Chengshilun yi shu 成實論義疏 (Dunhuang Pelliot 2335)."Saturday 2:00 to 5:00 pmChinese Exegesis II Chair: Lu Huang Wang Xingyi (Chinese University of Hong Kong): "Avijñaptirūpa in Abhidharma, Tattvasiddhi, and Its Rebirth in Yogācāra." Jackson Cole Macor (UC Berkeley): "Jizang's Critique of Abhidharma in the Sanlun xuanyi." Lin Qian (Qing Dao University): "Analysis of Mind in Zongjinglu: The Adoption of Abhidharma Methods in Chan Buddhism."Sunday 9:30 to 12:30 pmChinese Abhidharma Philosophy Chair: Robert Sharf Ernest Brewster (Austrian Academy of Sciences): "On the Nature and Existence of Cessation: Sinitic Analysis of Indic Intra-Abhidharma Debates." Bart Dessein (Ghent University): "Reflexivity in Chinese Abhidharma Texts" Yao Zhihua (Chinese University of Hong Kong): "On prajñaptisat."Sunday 12:30 to 1:00 pm Concluding Discussion

events.title: Ning Zheng: Molecular Glues: From Mechanisms to Therapeutics
events.description: Molecular glue (MG) degraders represent an exciting new modality in drug discovery highlighted by their ability to degrade undruggable targets and their favorable pharmacological properties. Thus far, only a very small number of MG degraders have been serendipitously found, most of which act on CULLIN4 E3 ubiquitin ligases. The scarcity of these novel compounds limits our understanding of their activity requirement, E3 ligases preference, and functional versatility, thereby hindering the prospective discovery of new MG degraders. In this presentation, I will highlight our latest studies on the identification of new MG degrader compounds as well as human disease mutations acting as genetic glues that foster neo-substrate-E3 interactions. These findings point to potential rational strategy for rational discovery of target-centric MG degraders.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)
